tabs.label: Building Rural
tabs.intro:
Thinking about building on rural land? This guide walks through the process from choosing a property to moving in.

If this is your first time building, this FAQ covers common questions and explains terminology. For general advice relating to building approval, you can call Council on 1300 697 372 — general enquiries are free.

items.q: Do I need approval to build on my rural block?
items.a:
Almost certainly yes. A new house, shed or carport needs building approval. Depending on the site, it may also need planning approval. The two are different. See What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?

More than a single house or shed? Start with Planning. If your project involves a second house or a granny flat, subdividing, farm-stay accommodation or a business, talk to our Planning team first. Where you need planning approval, you get it before building approval. On the Planning tab, see:
  • Can I build a second house (dual occupancy) on my rural land?
  • Can I build a granny flat (secondary dwelling) on my rural land?
  • Can I subdivide my rural land?
Or talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

A very short list of minor structures do not need building approval under Schedule 2 of the Queensland Building Regulation 2021. These are generally garden sheds under 10m², some retaining walls under 1m, and fences under 2m. They are called accepted development (self-assessable). This means you do not need building approval, but you are still responsible for meeting the Building Code of Australia, boundary setbacks and the Planning Scheme.

Do not rely on a summary for your project. What counts as exempt depends on exact sizes, where it sits on the lot, overlays, and what is already on the property. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 before you spend money. Getting this wrong can mean rebuilding.

Reference: Building Regulation 2021 — Schedule 2.

items.q: What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?
items.a:
They sound similar, but they answer 2 different questions:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It is about where the building goes, how it sits on the site, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. The rules cover setbacks, road access, distances from watercourses, overlays (flood, bushfire), and how close you are to things like quarries or feedlots.
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and does it meet the rules? It is about how the building is built: footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms, and all the engineering that makes it safe.

Many rural blocks have possible house sites that only need building approval, because the Planning Scheme already sets out acceptable outcomes. If your house site ticks every box on the Building a House in the Rural Zone checklist, you do not need planning approval and can go straight to building approval.

If your site does not tick every box (for example, it is in the bushfire zone or cannot meet setbacks), you need planning approval first, usually a Material Change of Use (MCU) application, and then building approval. See What if my site doesn't meet the Rural Zone Checklist?

items.q: How do I check whether my rural site is suitable before I spend money?
items.a:
Use these 2 free tools together. They tell you most of what you need to know before you talk to anyone.

  1. SDRC Online Mapping. Open the Online Mapping tool, search for your address and switch on the Planning module. This confirms your zone (such as Rural, Rural Residential or Township) and lets you turn overlays on and off, such as flood hazard, bushfire hazard, water resource catchment and airport environs. If your house site is in certain overlays, extra requirements apply.
  2. Rural Zone Checklist. Work through the Building a House in the Rural Zone checklist. It covers the "acceptable outcomes" (AOs) for setbacks, slope, a flood-free building site, water storage, distance from quarries, feedlots and abattoirs, energy supply, and overlay requirements.

If you can tick every item on the checklist, you do not need planning approval, just building approval. If you cannot tick an item, your site will need planning approval first (usually a Material Change of Use application). See What if my site doesn't meet the Rural Zone Checklist?

Rural Zone setbacks

Zone Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
Rural Zone 60m from all boundaries if gravel road frontage OR 6m from front & 60m from side & rear (if bitumen frontage) (or planning approval required) 6m from front boundary, regardless of road surface. 1.5m side & rear boundaries (or siting concession required)

Rural setbacks also interact with other things, such as watercourses, animal industries, slope and the size of a flood-free building pad. The mix is different for each block. For anything beyond the basics, talk to a duty planner, who will take you through what applies to your land. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: What if my site doesn't meet the Rural Zone Checklist?
items.a:
You apply for a Material Change of Use (MCU). This is a planning approval that assesses your proposal against the Planning Scheme's performance outcomes instead of the acceptable outcomes.

MCU (Material Change of Use): a type of planning application for when a land use is starting, restarting or intensifying. It applies here because rural houses that cannot meet all the acceptable outcomes become code assessable. They need planning approval before building approval.

If a performance outcome can be met another way, approval is usually granted with conditions. For example, if there is no constructed road to the property, a condition will be to build one. Or if there is a quarry nearby, conditions may require a building orientation or materials that reduce dust and noise.

What a simple MCU needs:

  • the application form (DA Form 1) and fees
  • the landowner's written consent
  • supporting information: how you will design, build and operate, and a statement addressing the Planning Scheme
  • details for each checklist item you do not meet

A code-assessable MCU is usually decided within 35 business days once the application is confirmed. Allow 2–3 months overall. It takes longer if we send an information request, if a Referral Agency is involved (we may need information from the State Government about your application), or if the application needs impact assessment.

Detailed guidance: How to Make a Material Change of Use

MCUs are technical. For anything beyond the simplest case, think about using a private town planning consultant. Or book a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with our Town Planners ($300, refunded if you lodge your application on time) for advice on your application. To talk to a duty planner, lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: Where do I start?
items.a:
For building in the Rural Zone, these are the usual steps:

  1. Choose a house site and decide what type of building you want. Rural blocks often have many possible house sites, some better than others. Different types of building (new build, prefabricated, removal home) each have pros and cons. A rough idea of what you will build, and where, makes it much easier to work out what approvals you need and to get quotes from contractors. Planning a second house or a granny flat? First see Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? on the Planning tab. The approvals depend on which one it is.
  2. Check whether you need planning approval. Open the Online Mapping tool and confirm your property is in the Rural zone. Then use the mapping tool to work through the Rural Zone Checklist. Mark each item ✓ / ✗ / NA.
  3. If any item is ✗, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. If you call, a Customer Service Officer will take some basic details before putting you through. General enquiries are free and you are not committing to anything. Have your address and your checklist, with any ✗ items, ready to discuss. You do not need to know all the terms before you call. That is what the duty planner is there for.
  4. Start getting quotes from licensed builders. This gives you a rough idea of what you can build within your budget and how long it might take. If you plan to use a private certifier, this is a good time to engage one. See Should I use a private certifier or Council for building approval?
Private professionals often have people they prefer to work with. For example, a builder may prefer a certain architect, building certifier or plumber. Who you choose to work with is up to you.

items.q: Should I use a private certifier or Council for building approval?
items.a:
It is your choice. You can hire a private certifier or use us as your certifier.

Building certifier: a QBCC-licensed professional who checks the building work against the Building Act, the National Construction Code, the Queensland Development Code and the relevant Australian Standards. They decide the application, arrange inspections, and issue the Form 21 Final Certificate at the end.

Using us as your certifier: you prepare and lodge the application yourself (or with your builder's help), and we do the assessment and inspections. This is usually cheaper overall, but more work for you.

Using a private certifier: most larger projects go this way. The certifier prepares and lodges the application for you. They usually bring in other professionals as needed (engineers, surveyors, soil tests, energy efficiency report, BAL report), deal with us for you, and do the on-site inspections. Our fees are the same either way. The certifier charges their own fee on top.

Many people find a private certifier is worth the fee. They can spot missing documents before you lodge, and plan the construction schedule around the certification process. As the applicant, it is up to you to decide what will work best.

If you choose us as your certifier, prepare your application and email it to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au. For any questions along the way, contact our building team on 1300 697 372. If you are using a private certifier, check they hold a current licence on the QBCC website.

items.q: What are the setback requirements?
items.a:
Setbacks are how far a building must sit from each boundary. They depend on the zone of your land and the class of building. For rural land, the 2 classes most property owners need to know about are:

  • Class 1a dwelling: a building designed for people to live in long term, such as a new house, a prefabricated home or a removal home.
  • Class 10a outbuilding: a building not designed for people to live in, such as a shed, garage, carport or workshop.

In the Rural Zone, dwellings and outbuildings have different setbacks:

Zone Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
Rural Zone If gravel road frontage, 60m from all boundaries. If sealed road 6m from front & 60m from side & rear (or planning approval required) 6m from front boundary, regardless of road surface. 1.5m side & rear boundaries (or siting concession required)

Class 1a dwellings: the 60m setback from every boundary on a gravel road surprises most people. The Planning Scheme aims to keep rural homes well away from unconstructed roads and neighbouring rural operations. On a bitumen road, the front setback is shorter (6m), but the side and rear setbacks stay at 60m. If your block cannot meet either pattern, you need planning approval. See What if my site doesn't meet the Rural Zone Checklist?

Class 10a outbuildings: sheds, garages and carports follow the same residential-style rule whatever the road surface. If you cannot meet 6m at the front or 1.5m at the side and rear, you can apply for a siting concession as part of the building application.

Other things often affect where you can build on rural land, such as distances from watercourses and animal industries, slope, and a flood-free building site. These do not change the setback rule above, but they do narrow down where on the block you can meet the approval rules. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 and ask for a call back from our Town Planning team to help find the best building position.

Rural Residential zone setbacks are not shown here. The rules are slightly different from the Rural Zone. If your land is Rural Residential (you can check by searching for the address on the Online Mapping tool), call our building team on 1300 697 372 for the correct setbacks.

items.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new rural house?
items.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling (new house or extension), you need:

  • a completed DA Form 2 (the Queensland Government building development application form)
  • a site plan, floor plan, elevations and structural details
  • the footing or slab design, with a Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • a soil test report
  • an energy efficiency report (houses must meet 7-Star)
  • a Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) report, if the site is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay
  • a QBCC Insurance Certificate, if you are using a licensed builder and the work is worth $3,300 or more, or a QBCC Owner Builder Permit, if you are building yourself and the work is worth $11,000 or more
  • a QLeave payment receipt, if the build is worth $150,000 or more (not including GST)
Once you have lodged your application, you cannot start any building work until you receive the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early, even clearing or pouring footings, creates unapproved work that has to be undone or certified after the fact at your cost.

Our Building Info Sheets have more information on the requirements. We reject incomplete applications, so check the right fact sheet before you lodge.

items.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new shed?
items.a:
For a Class 10a shed, you need:

  • a completed DA Form 2 (the Queensland Government building development application form)
  • a site plan, floor plan, elevations and structural details
  • the footing or slab design, with a Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • a Form 15 certificate for the steel frame, signed by an RPEQ
  • a QBCC Insurance Certificate, if you are using a licensed builder and the work is worth $3,300 or more, or a QBCC Owner Builder Permit, if you are building yourself and the work is worth $11,000 or more
  • a QLeave payment receipt, if the build is worth $150,000 or more (not including GST)

A shed does not automatically need a soil test. You may need one if the footing design calls for it, or if an engineering or on-site sewerage or plumbing approval applies.

You cannot start any building work until you receive the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early, even clearing or pouring footings, creates unapproved work that has to be undone or certified after the fact at your cost.

How this differs from a Class 1a house application: a shed does not need an energy efficiency report. It may still need to meet bushfire requirements if it is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay and within 6m of a home.

If you later apply for a house, that is a separate Class 1a application with the full list of documents. The shed does not "count" towards the house approval. They are assessed separately.

Our Building Info Sheets list the full requirements. We reject incomplete applications, so check the right fact sheet before you lodge.

items.q: What about sewerage? Do I need a septic tank or a treatment plant?
items.a:
Most rural properties are not connected to our sewerage network, so you will need an On-Site Sewerage Facility (OSSF) to treat wastewater on your own land. There are 2 main options:

  • Septic tank with an absorption trench: the traditional approach. Wastewater flows into the tank, solids settle, and liquid effluent soaks through trenches into the soil. It works well on land that drains well and has enough room for the trenches.
  • Aerated Wastewater Treatment System (AWTS): treats wastewater to a higher standard using air. This means the treated water can be spread over a smaller area, often by surface irrigation. It costs more to install and needs regular servicing, but is often the only option on smaller or difficult sites.

Which is right for your block depends on soil type, lot size, slope, distance from watercourses, bores and neighbours, and the number of bedrooms. A soil test and advice from a licensed plumber will give you a clear answer. Do not commit to a house design before this. The sewerage system can affect the size and position of the house.

You need our plumbing approval before installing an OSSF, and it is inspected during construction. Full details and application forms are on On-Site Sewerage Facilities (OSSF) — SDRC.

If your block is in one of our sewered areas, see Can I connect my property to Council's water and sewer? on the Water tab.

items.q: Can I plant a tree on the footpath or road reserve outside my property?
items.a:
Yes, with our permission. Lodge an online service request saying what you would like to plant and where. Our response will confirm whether you can go ahead. For help with the request, call us on 1300 697 372.

Our Street Tree Planting Guide lists trees and shrubs suited to footpaths and road reserves. The right choice depends on what is around it:

  • Near powerlines: choose a low-growing native from the guide's lists of plants that grow up to 2, 3 or 4 metres. As a rule of thumb, plant a tree as far from a power pole as it will grow tall.
  • Elsewhere: make sure it will not crowd a driveway, block the view at an intersection, get in the way of people walking, mail or bin collection, or affect a streetlight. The guide lists suitable species, including crepe myrtles.

items.q: What if I'm building a shed first, then a house later?
items.a:
This is a common approach in the Southern Downs. You build the shed first to store equipment and materials, then build the permanent house later. Both stages still need approval, and the process is similar for both.

A shed (Class 10a: sheds, garages, carports) needs its own building application, with a shorter list of documents than a new home:

  • a completed DA Form 2
  • a site plan, floor plan, elevations and structural details
  • the footing or slab design, with a Form 15 signed by an RPEQ
  • a Form 15 certificate for the steel frame, signed by an RPEQ
  • a QBCC Insurance Certificate or Owner Builder Permit (see What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new shed?)
  • a QLeave receipt, if the shed is worth $150,000 or more (not including GST)

A shed does not automatically need a soil test. You may need one if the footing design calls for it, or if an engineering or on-site sewerage or plumbing approval applies.

How this differs from a Class 1a house application: a shed does not need an energy efficiency report. It may still need to meet bushfire requirements (Australian Standard 3959) if it is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay and within 6m of a home.

When you later apply for the house, that is a separate Class 1a application with the full list of documents. See What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new rural house? The shed does not "count" towards the house approval. They are assessed separately.

items.q: What about tiny homes, prefabricated houses, or shipping container builds?
items.a:
A smaller or different type of building does not mean less approval. The most common misunderstanding is that "tiny" or "prefab" means the normal rules do not apply. They do.

Tiny homes

Fixed to the land. Whether prefabricated or built on site, a tiny home permanently fixed to the land and used as a main or secondary home is treated like any other Class 1a dwelling. It has the same building approval process, list of documents, inspections and Form 21 at the end. We removed the minimum floor area of 60m² in August 2024, so there is no "too small" limit for a Class 1 dwelling in the Southern Downs.

On wheels. These are treated like caravans. You can store one on the land without approval if it is genuinely just being stored (not lived in, and not connected to services). You can only live in one on your land with a Temporary Home permit. See Can I live on the land in a caravan or shed while I build?

Prefabricated and manufactured homes

These can be approved as Class 1a dwellings, but the paperwork is often harder, not easier. Many tiny homes and modular units sold commercially are imported and may not meet Australian standards. Before you buy, ask the supplier to confirm in writing that the building, plumbing and electrical work meet Queensland requirements, including RPEQ sign-off.

A certifier will want to check things like:

  • structural adequacy
  • ceiling height
  • energy efficiency (7-Star rating)
  • termite barriers
  • damp and weatherproofing
  • fire safety
  • a Form 15 for structural elements and a Form 43 for waterproofing
  • whether you can get QBCC insurance

If these certificates cannot be produced, you may not be able to get building approval. Without it, a Form 21 cannot be issued.

Shipping containers

It depends on what you will use it for:

  • Self-assessable (no approval): temporary short-term storage (under 6 months) on residential land during renovations or a move. It must not be fixed to the ground, must not be on a road or road reserve, and must not affect the amenity of the area. Short-term storage on industrial or rural land, or on an active building site, is also self-assessable.
  • Building approval needed: if you use it as an outbuilding (office, shed, workshop, hobby room) or as a structure (fence, viewing platform, architectural feature), store things in it long term (over 6 months), anchor it with footings or slabs, connect electricity or plumbing, or add doors, windows, awnings or other attachments.
  • Amenity & Aesthetics application: needed before building approval if the container is in any Urban or Rural Residential zone. It is also needed in the Rural zone if the container is within 100m of a residential area, on a lot of 4,000m² or less, or within 20m of a property boundary. Common conditions include painting, a concrete slab or 400mm stumps (so rabbits cannot shelter underneath, a Darling Downs-Moreton Rabbit Board requirement), and sometimes a pitched roof.

We have fact sheets on both tiny houses and shipping containers. The rules depend so much on your situation that you should call us on 1300 697 372 before you spend any money. A 10-minute conversation can save thousands.

items.q: What about removal homes (relocated houses)?
items.a:
Removal homes are popular in the region and have their own approval process. As well as a building approval, we act as a Concurrence Agency: we assess the house's condition and appearance, and require a security bond before the house can be moved.

The process is different enough that it has its own tab. See Removal Homes for the whole process: what to check before buying, the 2 applications, bond amounts and refunds, transport permits, and the inspections after the house arrives.

items.q: Do I need approval for my driveway?
items.a:
Yes, almost certainly. Any new or upgraded driveway has to cross our land (the road reserve, the strip between your property boundary and the road itself) to reach the road. Section 75(2) of the Local Government Act prohibits carrying out works on a road without our permission. That permission is called a Works Within Road Reserve approval. You need it as well as your building approval.

Road reserve: also called the nature strip. This is the full width of land set aside for a road, including the sealed or gravel surface, any verge or shoulder, table drains, and the strip up to the property boundary. We manage all of it, even though the verge and table drain may look like part of your property.

You need a Minor Works Within Road Reserve approval for:

  • a new driveway (part of almost every new build)
  • widening or moving an existing driveway
  • changing the driveway surface, for example from gravel to bitumen or concrete
  • any earthworks or culvert work in the road reserve, including filling in a table drain or putting in a new culvert pipe

What is involved:

  • Fill in the Application Minor Works — Works Within a Road Reserve form from our Engineering Department.
  • Attach a sketch or plan showing where in the road reserve the work will be.
  • Pay the application fee. See the current Fees & Charges schedule.
  • Allow 20 working days for assessment.
  • If approved, we send you an Approval Letter setting out the terms and conditions for the work.

Things to know on rural land:

  • Longer driveways often need a culvert where the driveway crosses the table drain, so water can keep flowing. We assess the culvert size and position as part of the approval.
  • Gravel driveways need approval too. The rule is about works on the road reserve, not whether the driveway is sealed.
  • If your property is on the New England Highway, Cunningham Highway or another state-controlled road, the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) assesses driveway access, not us. Call TMR's Darling Downs office on 07 4639 0777 before you apply to us.

Water or sewer pipes. If your driveway will pass over, or within 2m of, any of our water mains, sewer mains or manholes, you also need a separate Works Near Water Supply or Sewerage Infrastructure approval under Section 192(2) of the Water Supply (Safety and Reliability) Act 2008. That means a second form, a second assessment and a second fee. Our Engineering Department will tell you whether this applies when you first ask.

Many licensed driveway contractors include the Minor Works approval in their quote, but ask before you sign rather than assuming. Apply early. The Works Within Road Reserve approval is often a condition of building approval, so lodge it with (or before) your building application. Call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the Engineering Department for advice before you apply.

items.q: Existing Dwelling - Can I request a copy of my building plans or documents relating to past development applications?
items.a:
Yes. We keep an archive of all building plans in the Southern Downs region. This is useful if you want to renovate or extend, or just want a copy of the original plans for your property.

How to ask for a copy: email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au with:

  • the property address
  • the owner's name
  • roughly when it was built or approved, if you know
  • what you need, for example the decision notice, certificate or floor plans

Our Building team will get back to you to confirm what is available, talk through your options and arrange payment.

Fee: $71.00 per document. A Decision Notice, a Certificate or a set of Plans each counts as one document. We send plans with information on how they can be used, including copyright conditions.

The process is the same whether you are the current owner, a recent buyer, or a builder working on the property. For older records, our Building team can tell you what has been kept in the archive. Most records are available, but this varies for very old buildings.

items.q: What is a Form 15, Form 16, Form 43 and Form 21?
items.a:
These are standard certificates used throughout the Queensland building process. You will see them mentioned often:

Form 15 — Compliance Certificate for Building Design or Specification. Signed by an RPEQ (registered engineer) to confirm that part of the design meets the code. Commonly provided for footings, slabs and steel framing. Required before building approval can be issued.
Form 16 — Inspection Certificate. Signed by the building certifier (or another competent person) after each stage of construction, to confirm that stage passes. You will usually collect 4 of these over the build: footing, slab, frame and final.
Form 43 — Aspect Certificate (QBCC licensee). Filled in by the licensed tradesperson who did a particular part of the work, such as waterproofing or glazing, to confirm that part meets the building approval. It goes to your certifier, who can rely on it. Which ones are needed varies, so ask your certifier which they will want for your build.
Form 21 — Final Inspection Certificate. Issued by the certifier once the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met. It is the document that says the building is complete and lawful. For new dwellings, you cannot move in until the Form 21 is issued.

Your certifier manages all of these. Keep copies. They are important when you sell the house or change insurance. The forms are on Business Queensland's Building forms page.

To see which certificates your type of build needs, check its fact sheet on our Building Info Sheets page, or call our building team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What inspections happen during construction?
items.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling, the certifier must inspect and sign off 4 stages. Each stage must pass before the next one starts:

  1. Footing / Foundation: before the concrete is poured. Confirms the excavation depth, reinforcement and placement match the engineer's design.
  2. Slab: after the slab is prepared, before the pour. Confirms the reinforcement, plumbing penetrations and setout. Removal homes on footings usually skip this stage.
  3. Frame: once the framing (walls, roof structure) is up and before the sheeting goes on. Confirms tie-down, bracing and member sizes. Problems are often caught at this stage.
  4. Final: at completion. Covers everything: stairs, balustrades, smoke alarms, waterproofing, energy efficiency, safety and all conditions of approval.

Your builder usually arranges inspections directly with your certifier. Plumbing has its own inspections, done by our plumbing inspectors. Your plumber books those.

If a stage fails, the certifier gives you a written notice of what needs fixing. The work must be fixed and inspected again before construction continues. If a licensed builder refuses to fix defective work, the QBCC can issue a formal Direction to Rectify. See the QBCC website.

If we are your certifier and you have a question about an inspection, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: When can I actually move in?
items.a:
For a new dwelling, you can move in once the Form 21 Final Certificate has been issued. Not before, even if the house feels finished. The Form 21 is only issued after the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met.

Living in a new dwelling before the Form 21 is issued is an offence under the Building Act 1975. It can also affect your insurance.

Your builder arranges the final inspection with the building certifier. If we are your certifier and you have a question about the final inspection, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: Can I live on the land in a caravan or shed while I build?
items.a:
On rural land, yes, in a shed, caravan or mobile home. But only with our approval, and only after you have building approval for the permanent home. In an urban residential area, we can only approve a shed, not a caravan or mobile home.

The process:

  1. Get building approval for the home first.
  2. Fill in an Application for Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation and send it to us at least 30 days before you want to move in.
  3. Pay the fee.
  4. Send supporting information: drawings of the temporary home, a wastewater disposal plan, your drinking water supply (you need a tank of at least 5,000L), the landowner's consent if you are not the owner, and a clear reason why you need to live there temporarily.

We can approve it for up to 18 months, and may extend it to match when the permanent home is expected to be finished. The approval ends automatically when the home is finished, when the building approval lapses, or when the approval term ends.

A shed (Class 10a, with building approval already in place), caravan or mobile home can be approved as a temporary home. Full details are on SDRC — Temporary Homes.

Do not start living on site before you have approval. It can cancel the temporary approval altogether and lead to enforcement action.

For more information about applying for a temporary home permit, call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to our Development Compliance Officers.

items.q: How do I arrange rubbish collection once I've moved in?
items.a:
Kerbside collection does not reach every rural property. What happens depends on where your property is in our Designated Waste Collection Area:

  • Compulsory area: you do not need to ask. We arrange bins automatically once we have processed your Form 21 Final Certificate. The service is charged on your rates ($520 a year, 2026–27, whether or not you use the bins).
  • Opt-in / opt-out area: we will contact you to ask whether you want a service.
  • Voluntary area (outside the collection area): lodge a New waste bin for single unit dwelling request in our online request system. Cleanaway decides whether it can service the property, based on its route and access.

No kerbside service? You have 3 options:

  • a rural bin compound: a locked, shared facility. Residents in the catchment apply to us for a key
  • one of our waste facilities
  • a private waste operator: several service rural properties and can supply bins in different sizes
Cleanaway runs our kerbside collection under contract. It needs a Form 21 Final Certificate before it will start a service at a new home.

Call us on 1300 697 372 to check which area your property is in, or whether it is in a bin compound catchment. For the list of bin compounds, see I don't have a bin service — can I get one? on the Waste & Recycling tab.

items.q: Where do I get water if my tanks run low?
items.a:
Call a water carter. Many bulk water carting businesses deliver to rural tanks across the Southern Downs. We keep a list of approved water carters on the Approved Water Carters page.

If you want to check that a carter is licensed and approved to fill up at our filling stations, call us on 1300 697 372 and our staff can confirm.

Planning your water storage from the start saves money on carting over time. Rural homes must have on-site storage of 45,000L for 1–2 bedrooms, or 67,500L for more. These minimums are meant to get you through a normal dry spell without deliveries.

items.q: Can I offer farm-stay or cabin accommodation, or host campers, on my property?
items.a:
Yes, but start with planning. In the Rural zone, short-term accommodation (cabins, farm-stays) and tourist parks (caravan parks, camping grounds) always need planning approval:

  • Code assessment applies to:
    • short-term accommodation on at least 5 hectares with up to 2 buildings and 12 guests
    • short-term accommodation on at least 10 hectares with up to 4 buildings and 24 guests
    • a tourist park on at least 10 hectares with up to 20 sites
  • Anything bigger is impact assessable (public notification).

As well as planning approval, you will need:

  • building approval, for new buildings or to reclassify an existing house
  • a Local Law permit to operate
  • plumbing approval, if you add bathrooms

A bed and breakfast for up to six guests, run by the people who live on the property, is different. See Can I run a business from my rural property?

For full details, see Can I run short-term accommodation or a caravan park on rural land? on the Planning tab. To talk through your idea with a duty planner, lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: Can I run a business from my rural property?
items.a:
Yes. The Planning Scheme sets out which home-based businesses can run without planning approval. Generally, you do not need approval if the business has:

  • up to 100m² used for the business
  • residents plus no more than one employee who does not live on site
  • no more than two commercial vehicles, and no fuelling, servicing or repairing vehicles on site
  • no more than six clients at a time, 8am–7pm Monday to Saturday
  • one sign up to 0.3m², and no outside storage

Vehicle servicing or repair, shops, warehouses and transport depots are not home-based businesses. A bed and breakfast for up to six guests is. On rural land, it can be in a separate building at least 60 m from the side and rear boundaries. It needs a fire buffer of at least 40 m around it, kept clear of ground litter and dead trees.

For the full rules, see What approval is required to start a business from my home? on the Planning tab, or our Home Based Business fact sheet.

If your plans go beyond these limits, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Do I need permission to cut down a tree?
items.a:
It depends on whose land the tree is on.

On our land: trees on footpaths, road reserves and in parks are ours. Do not remove, prune or poison them yourself. If one of our trees is causing a problem or looks unsafe, lodge an online service request and we will assess it, or call us on 1300 697 372.

On your own property: you may still need approval to remove trees on your own land in some situations, for example:

  • where the land is in the Planning Scheme's biodiversity areas overlay (check your property on our Online Mapping tool)
  • where the vegetation is protected under State law, such as the Vegetation Management Act 1999 or the Nature Conservation Act 1992

If you are not sure whether your trees are affected, ask before you cut. Talk to a duty planner: lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: What costs and fees should I budget for beyond construction?
items.a:
As well as the construction itself, budget for these items when building a new rural home. For current prices, get quotes from the providers and check our current Fees & Charges schedule.

  • Our building application fee: see the current SDRC Fees & Charges.
  • Private certifier fee, if you use one.
  • Engineer (RPEQ): for the footing or slab design and Form 15, plus the soil test.
  • Energy efficiency assessment: required for all new homes.
  • BAL assessment: only if the site is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay.
  • QBCC Home Warranty Insurance: required for residential work over $3,300. Usually paid by the builder and added to the contract price.
  • QLeave levy: required for work over $150,000 (not including GST). It must be paid before building approval is issued.
  • Planning application fee: only if your site needs an MCU. This is separate from building fees.
  • Pre-lodgement meeting: optional. $300 for up to 1 hour with our planners, for advice on your project.
  • Infrastructure costs: rural sites often need a driveway, stormwater management, on-site water storage (45,000L for 1–2 bedrooms, 67,500L for more) and on-site sewage treatment. Get quotes early.
  • A second dwelling: a dual occupancy attracts infrastructure charges, and either type of second dwelling can change your rates. See How will a dual occupancy or secondary dwelling affect my rates and charges?

For help working out which of these apply to your project, call our building team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: Do I need approval to build on my urban block?
items.a:
Almost certainly yes. Any new dwelling, extension, carport, shed, deck, pool, or retaining wall over 1m needs building approval. Depending on what you are building and where, you may also need planning approval. The two are different. See What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?

More than a single house, extension or shed? Start with Planning. If your project involves a granny flat or second dwelling, subdividing, short-term accommodation or a home business, talk to our Planning team first. Where you need planning approval, you get it before building approval. On the Planning tab, see:
  • Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling?
  • Can I subdivide my land in a residential zone?
  • Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style)
  • What approval is required to start a business from my home?
Or talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

A very short list of minor structures do not need building approval under Schedule 2 of the Queensland Building Regulation 2021. These are generally garden sheds under 10m², some retaining walls under 1m, and fences under 2m. They are called accepted development (self-assessable). This means you do not need building approval, but you are still responsible for meeting the Building Code of Australia, boundary setbacks and the Planning Scheme.

Do not rely on a summary for your project. What counts as exempt depends on exact sizes, where it sits on the lot, overlays, and what is already on the property. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 before you spend money. Getting this wrong can mean rebuilding.

Reference: Building Regulation 2021 — Schedule 2.

items.q: What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?
items.a:
They sound similar, but they answer 2 different questions:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It is about where the building goes, how it sits on the site, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. On an urban block, you usually need planning approval for setback concessions, dual occupancies or secondary dwellings, or building in an overlay (flood hazard, heritage, character).
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and does it meet the rules? It is about how the building is built: footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms, and all the engineering that makes it safe.

Most simple houses on standard residential blocks in town only need building approval. Their setbacks and siting fall inside the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes, so no planning application is needed.

If you want to build closer to a boundary than the standard setback allows, add a second dwelling, or the site has an overlay, you may need planning approval first, and then building approval. For a granny flat or a second dwelling, see Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? on the Planning tab.

items.q: How do I check whether my urban block is suitable before I spend money?
items.a:
Use our free SDRC Online Mapping tool. It tells you most of what you need to know before you talk to anyone. Search for your address and switch on the Planning module. This confirms your zone and shows any overlays. The most common ones in town are:

  • Flood hazard: affects minimum floor levels and may mean an engineering assessment
  • Bushfire hazard: less common in the centres of Warwick and Stanthorpe, more common on the edges and in smaller towns. You may need a BAL (Bushfire Attack Level) report
  • Heritage or character: applies to some older parts of Warwick and Stanthorpe, and may add design and materials requirements
  • Airport environs: height limits near the Warwick airport
  • Easements: sewer mains, water mains and drainage easements often cross urban blocks and limit where buildings can go. Check before you decide where to build.

If no overlay applies and your build sits within the standard setbacks, building approval is usually all you need. See What are the setback requirements?

Each overlay brings extra requirements. For advice about your block, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: Where do I start?
items.a:
For building on an urban block, these are the usual steps:

  1. Decide what you want to build: a new house, an extension, a granny flat, a shed or a carport. A rough idea of what you will build, and where on the block, makes it much easier to work out what approvals you need and to get quotes from contractors.
  2. Check your zone and overlays on the Online Mapping tool. Most standard urban blocks fall within the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes, but overlays (flood, bushfire, heritage, character) will add requirements.
  3. If anything is not straightforward, such as setback concessions, a secondary dwelling or a block with an overlay, talk to a duty planner. (For a secondary dwelling, first see Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? on the Planning tab.) Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free. If you call, a Customer Service Officer will take some basic details before putting you through. Have your address and a rough description of what you want to build ready.
  4. After talking to the duty planner, you will know whether your build fits within the acceptable outcomes or needs planning approval. If you need planning approval and are not using a private planning consultant, think about booking a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with our Town Planners.
  5. Get 2–3 quotes from licensed builders. This gives you a rough idea of what you can build within your budget and how long it might take. If you plan to use a private certifier, this is a good time to engage one.
  6. If you are not using a private certifier, think about booking a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with our building certifier. They can help you prepare your building application and explain the standards your build must meet to pass inspection once construction starts.

At every step, our staff are happy to help you understand the process. It is not a test, and you do not need to know all the terms before you call. That is what the duty planner is there for.

Private professionals often have people they prefer to work with. For example, a builder may prefer a certain architect, building certifier or plumber. Who you choose to work with is up to you.

Connecting a new home or secondary dwelling to town water and sewer has its own application and fees. See Can I connect my property to Council's water and sewer? on the Water tab.

items.q: What are the setback requirements?
items.a:
Setbacks are how far a building must sit from each boundary. They depend on the zone of your land and the class of building. The 2 classes most property owners need to know about are:

  • Class 1a dwelling: a building designed for people to live in long term, such as a new house, a prefabricated home or a removal home.
  • Class 10a outbuilding: a building not designed for people to live in, such as a shed, garage, carport or workshop.

On urban blocks, setbacks come from the Queensland Development Code (QDC) and depend on lot size:

Lot size Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
450m² and over
(QDC MP 1.2)		 6m from front boundary, 1.5m from side & rear boundaries (or a siting concession is required) 1.5m from side & rear boundaries, subject to the QDC MP 1.2 A2(d) exemptions below for smaller outbuildings.
Under 450m²
(QDC MP 1.1)		 Smaller front and side setbacks apply, scaled to the lot. See the Queensland Housing Code for the exact numbers. Scaled to the lot. See QDC MP 1.1 / Queensland Housing Code, or call our building team.

Common exemptions for lots 450m² and over under QDC MP 1.2:

  • QDC MP 1.2 A1(c) — Open Carports may be within the road setback if both of these apply:
    • walls, solid screens and supports make up no more than 15% of the perimeter within the setback
    • there is no other place on the site that meets normal setbacks, allows vehicle access at least 2.5m wide, and has a maximum gradient of 1 in 5
  • QDC MP 1.2 A2(d) — Class 10a buildings (sheds, garages, carports) may be within side and rear boundary clearances if all of these apply:
    • the height is no more than 4.5m (or the mean height is no more than 3.5m)
    • the total length of all buildings along any one boundary is no more than 9m
    • they are no closer than 1.5m to a window in a habitable room of a neighbouring dwelling

If your design cannot meet standard setbacks and does not fit an exemption, you can ask for a siting concession as part of your building application. The certifier assesses it against the QDC's performance criteria, usually looking at the effect on the streetscape, overshadowing and privacy. A siting concession adds time and cost.

Not sure which zone your block is in? See How do I check whether my urban block is suitable before I spend money?, or look it up on our Online Mapping tool.

items.q: Should I use a private certifier or Council for building approval?
items.a:
It is your choice. You can hire a private certifier or use us as your certifier.

Building certifier: a QBCC-licensed professional who checks the building work against the Building Act 1975, the National Construction Code, the Queensland Development Code and the relevant Australian Standards. They decide the application, arrange inspections, and issue the Form 21 Final Certificate at the end.

Using us as your certifier: available for dwellings and extensions. You prepare and lodge the application yourself (or with your builder's help), and we do the assessment and inspections. This is usually cheaper overall, but more work for you.

Using a private certifier: most larger projects go this way. The certifier prepares and lodges the application for you, brings in other professionals as needed (engineers, surveyors, soil tests, energy efficiency report), deals with us for you, and does the on-site inspections. Our fees are the same either way. The certifier charges their own fee on top.

Many people find a private certifier is worth the fee. They can spot missing documents before you lodge, and plan the construction schedule around the certification process. As the applicant, it is up to you to decide what will work best.

If you choose us as your certifier, prepare your application and email it to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au. For any questions along the way, contact our building team on 1300 697 372. If you are using a private certifier, check they hold a current licence on the QBCC website.

items.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application?
items.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling (new house or extension), you need:

  • a completed DA Form 2 (the Queensland Government building development application form)
  • a site plan, floor plan, elevations and structural details
  • the footing or slab design, with a Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • a soil test report
  • an energy efficiency report (houses must meet the current energy standard, 7-Star)
  • a BAL (Bushfire Attack Level) report, only if the site is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay
  • a QBCC Insurance Certificate, if you are using a licensed builder and the work is worth $3,300 or more, or a QBCC Owner Builder Permit, if you are building yourself and the work is worth $11,000 or more
  • a QLeave payment receipt, if the build is worth $150,000 or more (not including GST)

Urban sites usually need fewer overlay reports than rural ones. Most blocks do not need a BAL report, bushfire protection measures, or much site-specific engineering beyond the standard. Our Building Info Sheets list the full requirements. We reject incomplete applications, so check the right fact sheet before you lodge.

Once you have lodged your application, you cannot start any building work until you receive the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early, even clearing or pouring footings, creates unapproved work that has to be undone or certified after the fact at your cost.

items.q: Can I plant a tree on the footpath or road verge outside my property?
items.a:
Yes, but ask us before you plant. Lodge an online service request saying what you would like to plant and where. Our response will confirm whether you can go ahead. For help with the request, call us on 1300 697 372.

Our Street Tree Planting Guide lists trees and shrubs suited to footpaths and road reserves. The right choice depends on what is around it:

  • Near powerlines: choose a low-growing native from the guide's lists of plants that grow up to 2, 3 or 4 metres. As a rule of thumb, plant a tree as far from a power pole as it will grow tall.
  • Elsewhere: make sure it will not crowd a driveway, block the view at an intersection, get in the way of people walking, mail or bin collection, or affect a street light. The guide lists suitable species, including crepe myrtles.

items.q: What about extensions, decks, sheds, and carports?
items.a:
Rules of thumb for common projects in town (always confirm your project with a certifier):

  • Extensions always need building approval. If the extension goes into a setback, you also need planning approval or a siting concession.
  • Decks and patios attached to the house need building approval. Decks more than 1m above natural ground level need balustrades that meet the Building Code.
  • Sheds over 10m² need building approval. Sheds under 10m² are self-assessable but must still meet the siting rules.
  • Carports need building approval. Open carports can sometimes sit within the front setback under QDC MP 1.2 A1(c). See What are the setback requirements?
  • Retaining walls over 1m high need building approval, with an engineering design and a Form 15.
  • Fences over 2m need building approval. Pool fencing has its own rules. See What about swimming pools?

For a quick yes or no on whether your project needs approval, call 1300 697 372.

items.q: Do I need approval for my driveway?
items.a:
Yes, almost certainly. Any new or upgraded driveway has to cross our land (the road reserve, including the footpath and verge) to reach the road. Section 75(2) of the Local Government Act prohibits carrying out works on a road without our permission. That permission is called a Works Within Road Reserve approval. You need it as well as your building approval.

Road reserve: the full width of land set aside for a road, including the sealed surface, kerb and channel, footpath and verge. We manage all of it, even though the footpath and verge may look like part of your front garden.

You need a Minor Works Within Road Reserve approval for:

  • a new driveway (part of almost every new build)
  • widening or moving an existing driveway
  • changing the surface (for example, gravel to concrete)
  • adding a second access point or a new kerb crossing

Simply resealing or maintaining an existing surface does not normally need approval.

What is involved:

  • Fill in the Application for Minor Works — Works Within a Road Reserve form from our Engineering Department.
  • Attach a sketch plan showing where the driveway will go, its size, and any drainage.
  • Pay the application fee. See the current Fees & Charges schedule.
  • Allow 20 working days for assessment.
  • If approved, we send you an Approval Letter setting out the conditions for the work.

Watch for water and sewer pipes. On urban blocks, water mains, sewer mains and manholes often run under footpaths and front yards. If your driveway will pass over, or within 2m of, any of our water or sewer infrastructure, you need a separate Works Near Water Supply or Sewerage Infrastructure approval under Section 192(2) of the Water Supply (Safety and Reliability) Act 2008. That means a second form, a second assessment and a second fee.

Signs of pipes below include meter boxes, sewer manholes, and valve or hydrant covers on or near the verge. Our Engineering Department will confirm what applies when you first ask.

Most licensed driveway contractors include both approvals in their quote, but ask before you sign rather than assuming. Apply early. The Works Within Road Reserve approval is often a condition of building approval, so lodge it with (or before) your building application. Call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the Engineering Department for advice before any concrete is poured.

items.q: What about swimming pools?
items.a:
Any pool that can hold water deeper than 300mm needs both building approval and pool fencing that meets the standard. This includes permanent pools, most portable and inflatable pools, spas, and portable wading pools that can hold that depth.

Pool safety in Queensland is covered by the Building Act 1975 and the Queensland Pool Safety Standard. The main points:

  • The pool must be registered on the Queensland Pool Safety Register.
  • You need a Pool Safety Certificate before selling or leasing a property with a pool, and whenever the fence is replaced or changed.
  • A licensed Pool Safety Inspector inspects pool fences, not us.
  • We can investigate unfenced pools, or pools that do not meet the standard, as a safety matter.

Full guidance, including pool fence specifications, how to report a pool that does not meet the standard, and registration, is on Swimming Pools — SDRC.

Drowning is one of the leading causes of accidental death for Queensland children under 5. Pool fencing rules are strictly enforced and there is no discretion on the standard.

items.q: Can I build a granny flat or secondary dwelling?
items.a:
The Planning Scheme rules for secondary dwellings are being reviewed and may change. Talk to a duty planner before you commit to a design or contract. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. The general advice below is confirmed, but the conditions for your project will depend on the scheme in force when you lodge.

Yes. A secondary dwelling (often called a granny flat) is a dwelling used together with the main house on the same lot, and secondary to it. It can be attached to the house, under it, or free-standing. In planning terms it is part of the house, not a second independent dwelling.

Whether you need planning approval depends on the zone. Under the current Planning Scheme (version 5):

  • Low Density Residential and Medium Density Residential zones: you do not need planning approval, unless the land is in the flood hazard overlay.
  • Township, Mixed Use, Rural Residential and Rural zones: you need planning approval (a Material Change of Use application).
  • Other zones: ask the duty planner.

You always need building approval and plumbing and drainage approval. The secondary dwelling must meet the Queensland Development Code and Planning Scheme requirements for a house, including site cover, setbacks and height. You do not need extra off-street parking. It cannot have its own title or be sold separately.

An extra bin service for a granny flat is charged on your rates. See How will a dual occupancy or secondary dwelling affect my rates and charges?

Renting it out. Since September 2022, a change to the Planning Regulation 2017 means you can rent a secondary dwelling to anyone, whether or not they are related to the people living in the main house. Before renting, check with a building certifier whether any building work is needed (particularly for fire safety). Check tenancy requirements with the Residential Tenancies Authority (RTA). The State Government has said it will review this change, so how secondary dwellings can be used may change.

A dual occupancy (duplex) is different. It is 2 independent dwellings on one lot for separate households, which can later be subdivided and sold separately. Dual occupancies in urban zones always need planning approval. See Do I need planning approval for a dual occupancy in a residential or rural residential zone? on the Planning tab.

Not sure which one you are building? See Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? The Dual Occupancy checklist has the current rules.

items.q: Can I request a copy of my building plans?
items.a:
Yes. We keep an archive of all building plans in the Southern Downs region. This is useful if you want to renovate or extend, or just want a copy of the original plans for your property.

How to ask for a copy: email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au with:

  • the property address
  • the owner's name
  • roughly when it was built or approved, if you know
  • what you need, for example the decision notice, certificate or floor plans

Our Building team will get back to you to confirm what is available, talk through your options and arrange payment.

Fee: $71.00 per document. A Decision Notice, a Certificate or a set of Plans each counts as one document. We send plans with information on how they can be used, including copyright conditions.

The process is the same whether you are the current owner, a recent buyer, or a builder working on the property. For older records, our Building team can tell you what has been kept in the archive. Most records are available, but this varies for very old buildings.

items.q: What is a Form 15, Form 16, and Form 21?
items.a:
These are standard certificates used throughout the Queensland building process:

Form 15 — Compliance Certificate for Building Design or Specification. Signed by an RPEQ (registered engineer) to confirm that part of the design meets the code. Commonly provided for footings, slabs and steel framing. Required before building approval can be issued.
Form 16 — Inspection Certificate / Aspect Certificate. Signed by the building certifier (or another competent person) after each stage of construction, to confirm that stage passes. You will collect 4 of these over the build: footing, slab, frame and final.
Form 21 — Final Inspection Certificate. Issued by the certifier once the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met. It is the document that says the building is complete and lawful. For new dwellings, you cannot move in until the Form 21 is issued.

Your certifier manages all of these. Keep copies. They are important when you sell the house or change insurance.

To see which certificates your type of build needs, check its fact sheet on our Building Info Sheets page, or call our building team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What inspections happen during construction?
items.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling, the certifier must inspect and sign off 4 stages. Each stage must pass before the next one starts:

  1. Footing / Foundation: before the concrete is poured. Confirms the excavation depth, reinforcement and placement match the engineer's design.
  2. Slab: after the slab is prepared, before the pour. Confirms the reinforcement, plumbing penetrations and setout.
  3. Frame: once the framing (walls, roof structure) is up and before the sheeting goes on. Confirms tie-down, bracing and member sizes. Problems are often caught at this stage.
  4. Final: at completion. Covers everything: stairs, balustrades, smoke alarms, waterproofing, energy efficiency, safety and all conditions of approval.

Your builder usually arranges inspections directly with your certifier. Plumbing has its own inspections, done by our plumbing inspectors. Your plumber books those.

If a stage fails, the certifier gives you a written notice of what needs fixing. The work must be fixed and inspected again before construction continues. If a licensed builder refuses to fix defective work, the QBCC can issue a formal Direction to Rectify. See the QBCC website.

If we are your certifier and you have a question about an inspection, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: When can I actually move in?
items.a:
For a new dwelling, you can move in once the Form 21 Final Certificate has been issued. Not before, even if the house feels finished.

The Form 21 is only issued after the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met. Common last-minute hold-ups are:

  • smoke alarms not interconnected
  • balustrades on decks over 1m not meeting the code
  • final stormwater discharge
  • any landscaping required by the approval conditions
Living in a new dwelling before the Form 21 is issued is an offence under the Building Act 1975. It can also affect your insurance.

Your builder arranges the final inspection with the building certifier. If we are your certifier and you have a question about the final inspection, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

Once the Form 21 is issued, you can also start kerbside bin collection. See I don't have a bin service — can I get one? on the Waste & Recycling tab.

tabs.label: Removal Homes
tabs.intro: Thinking about a removal home? Relocated houses are a popular and often cost-effective way to get a character home onto your block. The process is different from building new: as well as a building approval, Council acts as a Concurrence Agency — it assesses the amenity and aesthetic impact of the house, sets conditions, and requires a security bond that must be paid before the house can be moved. This tab walks through the whole journey, from checking the house before you buy it to getting your bond back at the end.

stepper.label: STEP 1
stepper.text: Get the house assessed — condition report + photos

stepper.label: STEP 2
stepper.text: Lodge building + concurrence applications

stepper.label: STEP 3
stepper.text: Council sets conditions and the bond

stepper.label: STEP 4
stepper.text: Pay the bond — Decision Notice issued

stepper.label: STEP 5
stepper.text: Move the house

stepper.label: STEP 6
stepper.text: Complete works, pass inspections, Form 21 — bond refunded

items.q: What is a removal home, and how is the approval different from building new?
items.a:
A removal home (or removal dwelling) is an existing house moved onto your land, or moved to a different spot on the same land. Both need a building approval. The building permit for a removal dwelling is valid for 12 months. Depending on the zoning of the land, you may also need a planning approval before a building permit can be issued.

The big difference from a new build is our extra role as a Concurrence Agency under the Planning Regulation 2017. A relocated house can affect the look and amenity of an area. So we assess its condition and appearance, put conditions on the approval, and set a security bond. You must pay the bond before the house is approved for relocation. The bond is your guarantee that the house will be brought up to an acceptable standard once it arrives.

Our Building Approval – Removal Dwellings and Concurrence Agency – Removal Buildings fact sheets set out the whole process. They are on the Building Info Sheets page. To talk through a particular house or block, call our building team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What should I check before buying a removal home?
items.a:
Two things catch people out, so check them before you hand over any money.

1. The condition report. Your application must include a report on the condition of the house against National Construction Code (NCC) requirements. It must be written by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ) or a Building Certifier. It has to cover:

  • whether the house is structurally adequate in its new location
  • the upgrades needed to bring it to current standards: tie down, bracing and strengthening to AS 1684.2
  • the condition of wet areas, external paint and roof sheeting
  • any deteriorated or termite-affected timber

Getting this report done early tells you what the house will really cost.

2. Asbestos. If the structure contains asbestos or material containing asbestos, you must get an exemption under Section 419 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 before it is moved. Workplace Health and Safety Queensland manages these exemptions. You must meet all the conditions they set in full.

Asbestos cement roofing must be removed and properly disposed of before the building enters the Southern Downs region.

You will also need recent photos of the house, showing every side and every room inside. They must clearly show the condition of the walls, roof sheeting and so on. If the seller cannot give you access for the report and photos, treat that as a warning sign.

For everything your applications will need, see What applications do I need to lodge, and what goes in them? If you have a question about a particular house before you buy, call our building team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What applications do I need to lodge, and what goes in them?
items.a:
You lodge 2 applications. You can email both to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au or lodge them over the counter at one of our Administration Centres. If you email them, a Customer Service Officer will contact you to take payment of the fee. Over the counter, you pay the fee when you lodge.

The building approval application should include:

  • a completed DA Form 2
  • a site plan, floor plan, elevations and structural details
  • the footing or slab design and a Form 15, signed by an RPEQ registered engineer
  • an Energy Efficiency Report
  • a Bushfire Attack Level Report, if the land is in a Bushfire Prone Zone
  • a Soil Test Report
  • a QBCC Insurance Certificate, if a builder or removalist is involved and the work is worth $3,300 or more, or a QBCC Owner Builder Permit, if you are doing the work yourself and it is worth $11,000 or more
  • a QLeave payment receipt, if the building work is worth $150,000 or more, not including GST

The amenity and aesthetics (concurrence agency) application should include:

  • a completed Application to Concurrence Agency (Removal Dwelling – Amenity & Aesthetics)
  • the engineer's or certifier's condition report, described in What should I check before buying a removal home?
  • recent photos of every side of the house and every room inside
We may reject an application if anything is missing. The Building Info Sheets set out the full requirements, so check them before you lodge.

items.q: How long does assessment take, and when can work start?
items.a:
Once you have given us all the information we need, we issue a Decision Notice within 35 business days.

Building approvals for removal dwellings are code assessable, and we assess them within the timelines in the Development Assessment Rules. If we need more information, we send an Information Request to the applicant named on the DA Form 2.

After assessment, we write to you with any conditions and the bond amount. Once you pay the bond, we issue the Decision Notice and work on moving the house can begin.

No work of any kind may start until we have issued a Decision Notice.

To lodge, email both applications to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au. See What applications do I need to lodge, and what goes in them? for what to include.

items.q: How much is the security bond?
items.a:
The bond depends on the zoning of the site the house is moving to:

Zone of the new siteSecurity bond
Rural Zone$15,000
Urban or Rural Residential Zone$30,000

After assessing your application, we confirm the exact amount and any conditions in our written Concurrence Agency advice. If you are happy with the conditions and want to go ahead, you then arrange to pay the bond.

The bonds are listed in our Fees & Charges schedule. To pay, see How do I pay the bond?

items.q: How do I pay the bond?
items.a:
You must pay the bond, and sign and return the Bond Agreement, before the house is moved. You can pay by:

  • bank transfer: the account details and reference number are on your removal building bond agreement
  • bank cheque: made payable to Southern Downs Regional Council
  • bank guarantee: this must be a signed and dated original, with no termination or expiry date. It must be unconditional and payable on demand, with a description (for example, "removal bond")
  • cash (not preferred)
We do not accept credit cards or personal cheques for removal building bonds.

Fill in the bond form in full and send it with your payment. We will only release the bond to the original payee shown on the receipt, so think about whose name it goes in.

Our building team will contact you to arrange payment. If you have a question about your bond agreement, call 1300 697 372 and ask for the building team.

items.q: How and when do I get the bond back?
items.a:
The bond is there to make sure the house is brought up to an acceptable standard. You get it back as you complete the work listed in your Referral Agency Response:

  • Partial refunds: we may release part of the bond as work progresses, at our discretion, depending on how much is complete. We consider each case on its own, and always keep up to 50% of the bond until final release. We cannot release a bank guarantee in part, only once all the work is complete.
  • Final release: this happens only once the Final Certificate (Form 21) has been issued after inspection.

There are fees for refund requests:

RequestFee
Partial refund — inspection required$509.00
Partial refund — no inspection required$255.00
Final release where work is not completed within 12 months of approval$509.00

To ask for a refund, send us a formal request with supporting documents.

For a partial release, include:

  • copies of the certificates for the completed work, including Form 12 or Form 16
  • photos of the completed stages
  • a list of the work still to do
  • the amount you are asking for

For final release, include a copy of the Form 21 from your Building Certifier.

Once we confirm your request is approved, fill in a "Refund or Transfer Payment Request Form – General" from our financial forms page. Email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. The request must come from whoever originally paid the bond. Include your application number, and give "full/partial refund of removal bond" as the reason.

items.q: Who arranges the transport permits for moving the house?
items.a:
Usually your removalist does. Before the building can be moved, the Police must issue a transport permit. That permit needs approval from both the Department of Transport and Main Roads and our Engineering Services.

You do not normally need to arrange these yourself, but check with your removalist that they have them in hand before moving day.

Once the house is on site, see What inspections happen once the house is on site — and when can I move in?

items.q: What conditions does Council typically put on a removal home approval?
items.a:
We set conditions for each application separately. These are the kinds of conditions to expect:

  • a building development application lodged with and approved by a building certifier
  • a plumbing and drainage application sent to us under the Plumbing and Drainage Act
  • the security bond paid and Bond Agreement signed before the building is moved
  • the base of the house enclosed with timber battens or other approved materials (gaps between battens no more than 50% of the batten width, 75mm from the ground)
  • the outside repainted so the paint protects the building materials from the weather
  • all defective or deteriorated materials replaced, repaired or made good. This commonly includes roof sheeting, roof battens, guttering and downpipes, damaged glazing and joinery, barge and fascia boards, eaves soffits, weatherboards (so the building is weatherproof), verandah flooring and stairs
  • other conditions that depend on the house you have chosen
If you disagree with a condition, you can ask your Building Certifier (the Assessment Manager) to pause the decision for up to 3 months while you make written representations to us. Ask the certifier within 10 business days of the response letter, and make your representations within the 3-month period. To discuss a response, contact our Planning and Development Department on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What inspections happen once the house is on site — and when can I move in?
items.a:
Once the house has been moved, the work must be completed in line with the Decision Notice conditions. Your Building Certifier must inspect these stages:

  • Footings: before the concrete is poured
  • Tie down: ideally while the roof is open and the wall frames are exposed
  • Final

When the house passes its final inspection, a Form 21 Final Certificate is issued and the bond refund can be arranged.

No one may live in the house until the Form 21 has been issued. Moving in early carries the same rule, and the same risk, as any other new build.

Book each inspection with your Building Certifier. If we are your certifier, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au. To get your bond back, see How and when do I get the bond back?

tabs.label: Planning
tabs.intro:
Thinking about a development — a new dwelling, a subdivision, a change of use, short-term accommodation, a commercial project? This page covers the planning side of development: what town planning is, when you need planning approval, and what the application process looks like.

Most questions can be answered over the phone with Council's duty planner — general enquiries are free. Call 1300 697 372.

stepper.text: Application — Council has 10 business days to confirm it's properly made

stepper.label: PART 2
