items.q: What is town planning, and do I need planning approval?
items.a:
Town planning manages how land is used, to create communities that work and last. It guides growth, protects the environment, and makes sure people can get services like water, waste and roads. In practice, it is the framework that decides what can be built where, and what has to be assessed before it is built.

Under Queensland's planning system, every development proposal falls into one of 3 categories:

  • Accepted: can go ahead without planning approval. A common example is a simple new house on a rural block that meets every acceptable outcome in the Planning Scheme.
  • Assessable: needs planning approval from us before it can go ahead. Most development that does not fit neatly inside the acceptable outcomes falls here.
  • Prohibited: not allowed under any circumstances. Only the State Government can make development prohibited, and it is rare.
Important: "Assessable" is not the same as "Prohibited". Most things that are not automatically Accepted are Assessable. This means they can be approved, just not without a formal planning application. If someone tells you "the Scheme does not allow it as Accepted development", that is not a refusal. It is a pathway.

Within Assessable, there are 2 further pathways:

  • Code Assessment: the application is assessed against the codes in the Planning Scheme that apply to your proposal. No public notification is needed, and most are decided by one of our planners under delegated authority.
  • Impact Assessment: applies to proposals that may have wider impacts on neighbouring land or the surrounding area. It needs public notification, and anyone can make a submission. Most are decided by our planning officers under delegated authority, but an application can be referred to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision.

The Planning Scheme decides which pathway applies. To see how your application would be assessed, look at the relevant codes on the Planning Scheme Codes page. Assessable development — what's the difference between Code Assessment and Impact Assessment? explains what each pathway means in practice.

"Do I need planning approval?" is the most common question our planning team gets. For most property owners, the fastest way to a reliable answer is:

  1. Check your zone and overlays on the Online Mapping tool.
  2. Work through the relevant checklist or fact sheet. We publish these for common situations, such as dwellings in the Rural Zone and dual occupancies in Residential and Rural Residential zones. Links to each are on the Planning Information Sheets page.
  3. If the checklist leaves any ✗ marks, or your situation is not covered by a checklist, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: What is the Planning Scheme?
items.a:
The Southern Downs Planning Scheme is the main document that sets out how land can be used across the region. It describes:

  • each zone (Rural, Residential, Rural Residential, Industry, Centre and others)
  • the overlays that apply to particular pieces of land (flood hazard, bushfire hazard, heritage, character)
  • the rules and outcomes a development has to meet to be approved

Importantly, the Planning Scheme is shaped by the community and the State. We do not write it on our own:

  • Community feedback: the Planning Scheme is developed and changed through public consultation. Residents, landholders, businesses, farmer groups and Landcare can make submissions during scheme reviews, and we consider those submissions before the scheme is finalised.
  • State regulators: the scheme must line up with Queensland's State Planning Policy and regional plans. These reflect State goals for housing supply, protecting farmland, environmental values and infrastructure. The State Government reviews and approves significant changes to the scheme.
  • Us: we manage the scheme day to day, assess development applications against it, and lead the review process for the region.

Because of these 3 parties, planning decisions sometimes feel more limited than we would like, and sometimes more flexible than the community might expect. Neither we nor residents set the rules alone.

The current scheme and supporting documents are on our Planning & Development page.

The Planning Scheme is changing. A new draft Southern Downs Planning Scheme was open for public consultation from 28 July to 19 September 2025, and we endorsed the draft in December 2025. You can read the draft, the consultation report and the proposed zone changes at haveyoursay.sdrc.qld.gov.au/draft-southern-downs-planning-scheme. We will keep deciding current applications under the existing scheme until the new one is formally adopted.

items.q: What's the difference between planning approval and building approval?
items.a:
They sound similar, but they answer 2 different questions:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It is about where the development goes, how it sits on the site, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. Planning looks at setbacks, road access, mapping overlays (such as flood and bushfire), whether the use fits the zone, and the effect on neighbouring properties and the wider area.
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and does it meet the rules? It is about how the building is built: footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms, and all the engineering that makes it safe.

A useful way to think about it: Planning deals with the land, and Building deals with the structure on it. They are 2 separate teams, 2 separate processes and 2 separate sets of forms.

Many simple developments only need building approval, because the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes already cover them. For example, a new rural house that meets every item on the Rural Zone Checklist, or a standard house in town within standard setbacks on a standard block, can usually go straight to building approval.

You need planning approval when the proposal does not fit the acceptable outcomes. For example, the setbacks cannot be met, the use (such as a dual occupancy) is not accepted development in that zone, or you want to subdivide. In those cases, you must get planning approval before building approval. The building certifier will want to see the planning approval before they can assess the building application.

If you are building a simple house, the Building Rural or Building Urban tab is a great place to start. If your project involves anything more, such as a subdivision, a second dwelling, a change of use, short-term accommodation or a commercial project, you are in planning territory, and the rest of this tab is for you.

items.q: What type of planning application do I need?
items.a:
It depends on what you are proposing. Four types of planning application cover almost everything residents in the Southern Downs need to lodge:

Reconfiguration of a Lot (RC): changing lot boundaries. This includes subdivision (creating 2 or more separate lots, each with its own title), boundary realignment, and creating access easements. If lot lines are changing, it is an RC.
Subdivision: a type of Reconfiguration. Specifically, splitting one lot into 2 or more new lots, each of which can be sold separately with its own title. Subdivisions are assessed against the Planning Scheme's minimum lot size, access and servicing requirements for the zone. Approval usually comes with conditions requiring infrastructure works (road, water, stormwater).
Material Change of Use (MCU): a planning application for a change in how a property is used. The Planning Act 2016 defines an MCU as (a) the start of a new use, (b) the re-establishment of a use that has been abandoned, or (c) a material increase in the intensity or scale of an existing use. Common Southern Downs examples are starting short-term accommodation (Airbnb-style), approving a house site that cannot meet standard setbacks, dual occupancies, granny flats outside the Low and Medium Density Residential zones, and commercial or industrial uses on land not already zoned for them.
Operational Works (OPW): an application for engineering work that materially affects the land, such as earthworks, roads, drainage, and water and sewer mains. It is often required by the conditions of an MCU or RC approval, such as the roads and services in a subdivision. See What is operational works, and when do I need approval?

Some examples:

  • A new rural house that cannot meet setbacks may only need a single MCU application.
  • A subdivision into 6 lots needs an RC.
  • Turning a rural property into farm-stay accommodation needs an MCU.
  • A development that changes boundaries and changes use needs both an RC and an MCU, often lodged together.
  • A subdivision that needs new roads or services usually also needs Operational Works approval, once the RC is approved.

If you are not sure which type applies, describe your proposal to a duty planner and they will tell you. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: How do I make a planning application?
items.a:
The Queensland planning application process has 5 main parts. Not every application goes through every part: referral, information requests and public notification only happen in some cases.

To be "properly made", a typical application needs:

  • a cover letter
  • a DA Form 1, the standard Queensland Government development application form
  • plans: site plan, floor plans and elevations (an architect, surveyor or similar professional can prepare these)
  • signed Owner's Consent (there is a template on the Queensland Government forms page)
  • the application fee. Once you know the application type, you can find the fee on our Fees & Charges page

To help work out what supporting documents your application may need, see the Planning Scheme Codes page, or talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

Application — we have 10 business days to confirm it is properly made
Referral to State agencies (if applicable)
Information request (if applicable) — you have up to 3 months to respond
Public notification (Impact Assessment only) — at least 15 business days
Decision — usually 35 business days, and can be extended

Part 1 — Application. We have 10 business days to confirm your application is properly made. If it is, we issue a Confirmation Notice. If it is not (for example, documents or consent are missing, or the fee is wrong), we issue an Information Request listing what is missing. The clock does not start until the problems are fixed.

Part 2 — Referral. If your proposal needs to be referred to a State agency, you (the applicant) send it directly to the referral agency, not to us. The main referral agency is the State Assessment and Referral Agency (SARA). Common reasons for referral include:

  • land within 25 metres of a state-controlled road (for example, the New England or Cunningham Highway)
  • clearing, or being close to, regulated or protected vegetation
  • proposals involving a concurrence Environmentally Relevant Activity (ERA)
  • land on the Queensland Heritage Register

This list is not complete. You may have to pay extra fees to us and, separately, to the referral agency. The referral agency has its own assessment period, which adds time. The duty planner or a private planning consultant can tell you what to expect for your proposal.

The clock pauses. When the process is waiting on a State referral agency, a planning consultant, a surveyor, an engineer or the applicant, the legal timeframes pause. If a decision feels slow, it is usually because the application is waiting on someone else for a response or a document. Check the current status in the Application Tracking Tool before assuming we are the hold-up.

Part 3 — Information Request. We may send an information request asking for more material, such as extra documents, a traffic impact assessment or engineering reports. The applicant then has up to 3 months to respond.

Part 4 — Public Notification. For Impact Assessment applications only. The applicant runs the notification process. We provide the signs, but the applicant is responsible for putting a sign on every frontage, a newspaper notice, and writing to neighbouring owners. The period runs for at least 15 business days. During this time anyone can make a submission for or against the application. See How do I object to a planning application near me?

Part 5 — Decision. We then have 35 business days to decide the application. The decision period can be extended in some cases, for example by agreement with the applicant.

Most planning applications, including many impact-assessable ones, are decided by our planning officers under delegated authority. The Chief Executive Officer, a General Manager or the Manager can instead refer an application to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision. If your application is referred to a Council meeting, we will tell you the date before the meeting agenda is released. You can ask to address Councillors at the meeting, in line with our Meeting Policy.

Once the application is decided, the applicant receives a Decision Notice. A 20-business-day appeal period follows, during which the applicant can either:

  • Request a Negotiated Decision by making "change representations" to us, asking for specific conditions of approval to be reviewed or changed. This is a useful first step if only some conditions are a problem.
  • Lodge an appeal in the Planning & Environment Court against the conditions, or against a refusal.

For impact-assessable applications, people who made a properly made submission can also appeal an approval to the Planning & Environment Court, within the appeal period stated in the decision notice.

Approval currency periods: an approval lapses if the development has not happened by the end of its currency period. The usual periods are below, but check your decision notice, which states the period that applies:

  • MCU (Material Change of Use): 6 years for the approved use to start
  • RC (Reconfiguration of a Lot): 4 years to lodge the plan of subdivision with us
  • BA + OPW (Building / Operational Works): 2 years for the work to substantially start

You must also keep meeting the conditions of approval during the currency period and after it. When you are ready to start the approved use, contact us to arrange a compliance inspection. This confirms the conditions have been met and reduces the risk of enforcement action later.

items.q: Assessable development — what's the difference between Code Assessment and Impact Assessment?
items.a:
If a proposal is assessable (it needs planning approval), the Planning Scheme puts it on one of 2 assessment pathways:

  • Code Assessment is the simpler pathway. The application is assessed against the codes in the Planning Scheme that apply to the proposal. No public notification is needed. Most code-assessable applications are decided by one of our planning officers under delegated authority.
  • Impact Assessment applies to proposals that may have wider impacts on neighbouring land uses or the surrounding area. Impact Assessment needs public notification: the applicant must put up signs on every frontage, advertise in the newspaper and notify neighbouring owners. Anyone can make a submission for or against. Most planning applications, including many impact-assessable ones, are decided by our planning officers under delegated authority. The Chief Executive Officer, a General Manager or the Manager can instead refer an application to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision.

The Planning Scheme decides which pathway applies. It is not a choice the applicant or we make when the application is lodged. Generally, uses that fit the zone's intent get Code Assessment. Uses at the edge of or outside the zone's intent get Impact Assessment.

Your planner or the duty planner can confirm which pathway your proposal is on before you lodge. It is worth knowing early. Impact Assessment adds at least 15 business days to the timeline for public notification alone, plus the cost of signs and advertising.

To find out which pathway applies to your proposal, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: General enquiry vs Pre-Lodgement Meeting — which do I need?
items.a:
It depends how specific your question is. There are 2 ways to talk to our planning team before you lodge an application.

General Enquiry: free. Best for open questions like "what can I do with this block?", "is this use even possible here?" or "which pathway applies to my idea?". Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. Good for:

  • the opportunities and limits of a particular site
  • checking where a proposed building could go
  • exploring what a piece of land might be used for
  • understanding terms or application requirements before you commit

Pre-Lodgement Meeting: $300. Best if you have a clear, specific development goal and want advice on this particular proposal before lodging a formal application. The meeting helps you understand the main areas of assessment, the likely conditions, and what supporting documents you will need.

The $300 fee is credited back to the application. If you lodge an application within 12 months of the pre-lodgement meeting, under the same Planning Scheme, for the same land and the same type of development, we credit the $300 against your application fee. Include a copy of the pre-lodgement receipt with the application to claim the credit. The credit applies once per site or proposal. Further pre-lodgement meetings on the same matter do not add up.

Practical details:

  • Booking: fill in the Pre-lodgement Request Form and email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. One of our officers will contact you with payment details. We schedule the meeting once you have paid.
  • Wait time: allow up to 4 weeks for the meeting to be scheduled. Our planning staff need time to review your concept plans and prepare advice. Book early.
  • Length: usually 30 minutes, and no more than 1 hour.
  • Location: online through Microsoft Teams, in person at our Warwick office (usually Wednesday at 2pm or 3pm), or in person at Stanthorpe on request. Up to 5 people in person, or any number on Teams.
  • What to bring: the request form with your questions listed, property details (address, lot and plan, current use, lot size), a description of the proposal, and a site plan. A hand-drawn plan is fine at this stage, as long as it clearly shows boundaries, existing structures and distances.
  • After the meeting: we email you a record of what was discussed within one week.
  • Confidentiality: what is discussed at a pre-lodgement meeting is treated as commercial in confidence. We do not release the meeting record to anyone who was not there without your permission.
  • Councillors: if you would like a Councillor to attend, you must ask through the Chief Executive Officer's office. No more than 2 Councillors can attend, and only as observers. They cannot comment on the proposal or the advice given.

Be aware: SARA runs its own process. If your proposal raises State interests (see the state-controlled road, vegetation, ERA and Heritage Register points in How do I make a planning application?), the State Assessment & Referral Agency (SARA) offers its own pre-lodgement meetings to confirm which State codes apply. Book with SARA directly, through its Toowoomba office on 07 4616 7307. For complex rural proposals near highways or regulated vegetation, it is often worth having both a pre-lodgement meeting with us and one with SARA.

A simple test: if you are still exploring options, start with a general enquiry. If you already have a firm plan and want to refine it before lodging, book a pre-lodgement meeting.

Pre-lodgement advice is not a promise to approve. Advice given at a pre-lodgement meeting cannot override our legal responsibilities during formal assessment. These include considering public submissions, referral agency responses, and anything that comes to light during detailed assessment. A pre-lodgement meeting reduces surprises, but it does not guarantee an outcome.

items.q: Can I run a bed and breakfast from my home?
items.a:
Yes. A B&B (guest accommodation run by the people who live in the home) is a home-based business under the Planning Scheme. In the Low Density Residential, Medium Density Residential, Rural Residential, Township and Rural zones, it does not need planning approval if it takes no more than six guests and meets the scheme's requirements:

  • In the Low and Medium Density Residential zones, the guest rooms are under the same roof as the home.
  • In the Rural Residential and Rural zones, the guest accommodation can be in one separate building. In the Rural zone, it must be at least 60 m from the side and rear boundaries.
  • There are 2 car parks for the residents, plus 1 for each guest bedroom.
  • The area around the B&B is landscaped and safe for guests. On rural land, a fire buffer of at least 40 m around the building is kept clear of ground litter and dead trees.

The home-based business limits on floor area and client hours do not apply to a B&B. More than six guests needs a code-assessable planning application. In other zones, it is case by case, so ask the duty planner.

Planning is only one layer. The building, Local Law and food approvals in What approvals are required for short-term accommodation? still apply. Every B&B needs a change of building classification to Class 1b (see When does my house need to be reclassified to Class 1b?).

Letting a whole house with no one living there (Airbnb-style) is not a B&B. See Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style)

To check your plans against the rules, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: What approvals are required for short-term accommodation?
items.a:
Short-term accommodation (Airbnb-style lets, B&Bs, holiday cabins, motels, farm-stays, caravan parks) often needs more approvals than people realise. Think of it as a stack of separate approvals, not a single application. Usually 3 apply, sometimes 4:

  1. Planning approval: sometimes needed, depending on the zone, the scale and the number of guests. Often not needed to let an existing house in town to a small number of guests.
  2. Building approval to reclassify the dwelling from Class 1a to Class 1b: needed whenever an existing house is used for short-term accommodation, even when no building work is involved. See When does my house need to be reclassified to Class 1b?
  3. Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation: usually needed.
  4. Plumbing & drainage approval: only needed if your conversion involves plumbing work.
This change will affect the rates and charges for your property. Once a property is reclassified for short-term accommodation, it moves to a different rates category. Contact our Revenue Department for the details before you commit.

Where to next?

  • Letting an existing house in town for short stays (Airbnb-style)? See Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style)
  • Cabins, farm-stay, motel-style accommodation or a caravan park on rural land? See Can I run short-term accommodation or a caravan park on rural land?
  • A bed and breakfast for up to 6 guests in the home you live in? See Can I run a bed and breakfast from my home?

For anything that looks borderline, or to talk through your idea before you commit, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: When does my house need to be reclassified to Class 1b?
items.a:
Whenever you use it for short-term accommodation. Every building is classified under the National Construction Code by how it is used. A house you live in is Class 1a. Using it for short-term accommodation changes it to Class 1b, a small guest accommodation building with extra fire safety requirements. The change needs its own building approval, even if no building work is involved.

This applies to any short-term accommodation, including:

  • a bed and breakfast: guests stay in your home while you live there
  • letting a whole house for short stays (Airbnb-style)
  • cabins or farm-stay buildings: where four or more are on one lot and used for short-term holiday accommodation, each one is Class 1b, whatever its size

Class 1b covers guest accommodation for up to 12 people, with up to 300m² of floor area in total. Anything bigger is a commercial building with different requirements. Talk to a building certifier.

The change usually means:

  • interconnected smoke alarms in every bedroom and the hallways serving them
  • lighting that comes on with the alarms
  • stairs and balustrades that meet the code
  • where 4 or more bedrooms are offered to guests, an accessible bedroom and bathroom

You lodge a building application, and we decide it within 35 business days of having everything we need. Once the building passes inspection, you can apply for the Local Law permit to operate. The full steps are in Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style). The reclassification fact sheet is on our Building Info Sheets page.

To check what your property needs, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style)
items.a:
Most likely yes. In planning terms, this is the most permissive path in the scheme. This answer covers properties in the Low Density Residential and Medium Density Residential zones. Check your zone by searching for the property address on the Online Mapping tool.

Renting out an existing house needs 3 approvals, and sometimes a fourth. What approvals are required for short-term accommodation? sets out the full stack. This answer explains each one as it applies in town.

Planning approval: often not needed

You generally do not need planning approval if all of these are true:

  • the accommodation is in an existing dwelling (not a new build, and not a building that is not a dwelling, like a converted shed)
  • no more than 6 guests stay at any one time
  • the proposal meets the acceptable outcomes in the Planning Scheme (parking, amenity, signs, hours and similar)

If you cannot meet every acceptable outcome, you need a code-assessable planning application. If you want more than 6 guests, a new accommodation building, or to use a building that is not a dwelling, the application becomes impact-assessable. That means public notification, and the application may be referred to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision.

Building approval: reclassification from Class 1a to Class 1b

This surprises a lot of operators. Under the Building Act 1975, an existing house is Class 1a (a dwelling). Using it for short-term accommodation changes it to Class 1b (a small guest accommodation building). See When does my house need to be reclassified to Class 1b? The reclassification is a separate building approval, needed even if no physical building work is happening. The new class brings requirements designed for paying guests rather than residents:

  • Smoke alarms: interconnected hard-wired alarms, in or near the ceiling, in every bedroom and every corridor linked to bedrooms.
  • Evacuation lighting: lighting set off by the smoke alarm to help people get out. You can use existing lighting if it is wired to come on with the alarm.
  • Balustrades and stairs: needed for any landing, verandah or deck floor more than 1m above the ground, meeting current Building Code of Australia standards.
  • Disabled access: needed to one bedroom and its bathroom where there are 4 or more guest bedrooms, plus access to shared rooms.
  • Properties in the bushfire overlay: extra requirements apply, as set out in the Development in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay fact sheet.

How to lodge:

  • Email it to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au, or lodge it in person at one of our Administration Centres.
  • Include a completed DA Form 2, a site plan (north point, existing buildings, distances to boundaries) and a floor plan (showing smoke alarms, escape lighting, and entrance and exit doors). Also include a QBCC Insurance Certificate (if a builder is involved and the work is worth $3,300 or more) or a QBCC Owner Builder Permit (if you are doing the work yourself and it is worth $11,000 or more).
  • We issue a decision within 35 business days of having all the information. After our certifier inspects the building and finds it meets the standards, we issue a Form 11 Certificate of Classification (sometimes called a certificate of occupancy). (This is different from the Form 21 final inspection certificate issued for a new house.)
  • Once the Form 11 is issued, you can apply for the Local Law permit (the next step).

Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation

You apply for this after the building reclassification is complete. It is managed under our Local Law. See the Licences & Permits for Business page for the application form and current fee.

Plumbing & drainage approval (if needed)

If your reclassification involves any new bathrooms, ensuites, extra fixtures or changes to existing plumbing, you need a separate plumbing and drainage application. If there is no plumbing work, you do not need this approval.

Other things worth knowing

  • Food licence: if you serve any food (breakfasts, packaged snacks, mini-bar items prepared on the premises), you need a separate Food Business Licence under the Food Act 2006. See Do I need a licence to sell food or offer beauty services from home?
  • Rates and charges change once the property is reclassified. See What approvals are required for short-term accommodation?

The building reclassification fact sheet is on our Building Info Sheets page. The planning fact sheets on short-term accommodation, with their acceptable outcomes checklists, are on the Planning Information Sheets page.

For anything that looks borderline, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Can I run short-term accommodation or a caravan park on rural land?
items.a:
Yes, but it takes more than in town. In the Rural zone, planning approval is always needed. The building reclassification, Local Law permit and other approvals in What approvals are required for short-term accommodation? all still apply on top.

A bed and breakfast for up to six guests, run by the people who live on the property, is different. It is a home-based business and often does not need planning approval. See Can I run a bed and breakfast from my home?

There are 2 separate uses on rural land:

  • Short-term accommodation: cabins, farm-stay, and motel-style accommodation in buildings.
  • Tourist parks: caravan parks and camping grounds.

Cabins, farm-stay, motel-style accommodation

Your lot size and the number of buildings and guests decide which planning pathway applies:

  • Code assessable: if your lot is at least 5 hectares, you have no more than 2 accommodation buildings, and no more than 12 guests at any one time.
  • Code assessable: if your lot is at least 10 hectares, you have no more than 4 accommodation buildings, and no more than 24 guests at any one time.
  • Impact assessable: anything outside those 2 brackets.

Code-assessable applications are decided by a planner under delegated authority and do not need public notification. Impact-assessable applications need public notification and may be referred to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision. They take longer and cost more, so discuss them with the duty planner before you lodge.

Caravan parks and camping grounds (tourist parks)

  • Code assessable: if your lot is at least 10 hectares and you have no more than 20 sites.
  • Impact assessable: anything larger, or on a smaller lot.

Tourist parks have an extra ongoing layer. Once approved, they operate under our Caravan Parks Local Law, which covers things like the number of amenities, dump points and waste management. The duty planner will point you to those requirements early.

The other approvals still apply

  • Building approval: needed for any new accommodation buildings. You may also need a Class 1a to 1b reclassification if you are using or converting an existing house. See Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style) for what the reclassification involves. The same standards apply on rural land, and bushfire overlay requirements are more likely to be relevant.
  • Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation: usually needed.
  • Plumbing & drainage approval: for new bathrooms, amenities blocks, or significant changes to existing plumbing.
  • State environmental approvals may apply for larger sites without town sewerage, which is common on rural land. The duty planner can tell you what is likely to apply.
  • Food licence: you need a separate licence under the Food Act 2006 if you serve any food.

Rates and charges change once a property is reclassified for short-term accommodation. See What approvals are required for short-term accommodation?

Rural accommodation often involves bushfire overlays, setbacks from watercourses and on-site sewerage, which affect what is possible on a particular block. We strongly recommend booking a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with our Town Planners before you spend significant money on plans. The fee is small compared with what it can save you in redesign or refusal.

To discuss your situation with a duty planner, lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: Can I subdivide my land in a residential zone?
items.a:
Possibly. Unlike rural land, residential land is where we expect new lots to be created, so subdivision is often supported, as long as each new lot meets the requirements for its zone.

Some terms you will come across:

  • Reconfiguring a lot (RC): the planning term that covers subdivision. It also covers combining 2 or more lots into one, and moving the boundaries between lots. Most subdivisions and boundary realignments need a development approval.
  • Minimum lot size: applies to each lot you create, and is set by your zone (and in some zones, your town). If a lot cannot meet it, the application is assessed at a different, usually harder, level.
  • Rear lot: a lot behind another lot, reached by a narrow access strip (often called a battle-axe lot). The access strip does not count towards the lot's minimum size.
  • Plan of Subdivision (survey plan): the plan your surveyor prepares once the conditions of approval are met. We endorse it, and it is then lodged with the Titles Office to create the new titles.

Where to start: find your zone on the Online Mapping tool, then read our Subdivision in Residential Zones fact sheet. It covers the Low density residential, Medium density residential, Township and Rural residential zones. For each, it sets out the minimum lot sizes, the site requirements (slope, flood-free building area, access), the infrastructure you are likely to have to provide, timeframes, and the fees to budget for.

Subdivisions often need more than the RC approval. New roads, footpaths, water, sewer or stormwater connections, earthworks and street lighting may also need operational works approval. See What is operational works, and when do I need approval?

Once you have read the fact sheet, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. For the application itself, see How do I make a planning application?

items.q: Can I subdivide my rural land?
items.a:
In most cases, not easily. In line with State Government Planning Policy, subdivision in the Rural Zone is generally not supported. The Southern Downs Planning Scheme sets minimum lot sizes for rural land. They are large enough to keep productive farms viable and to discourage breaking rural land up into rural residential lots. If your land is below the minimum for its rural precinct, subdivision is unlikely to be approved. It is not impossible, if an Impact Assessment application can show enough merit.

If your land is in a residential zone, see Can I subdivide my land in a residential zone?

Minimum lot sizes by rural precinct. Each new lot must meet the minimum for its precinct:

PrecinctMinimum lot size
Alluvial Plains200 hectares (~494 acres)
Basalt Quality Grazing200 hectares (~494 acres)
Basalt Uplands200 hectares (~494 acres)
Granite Belt100 hectares (~247 acres)
Granite Hills500 hectares (~1,235 acres)
Granite Plains500 hectares (~1,235 acres)
Sandstone Rises & Traprock Hills700 hectares (~1,730 acres)
Walloon Arable200 hectares (~494 acres)

Find your planning zone by searching for the property on the Online Mapping tool. The planning module shows the zone and many of the relevant overlays. Use the Rural Precinct Overlay to find your property's rural precinct, or see the Rural Zone Precincts Map.

There is no "family" exemption. We do not make exceptions for subdivisions meant for a family member, such as a child building a house, a parent downsizing, or succession planning. We assess every subdivision application against the same minimum lot sizes, whoever the new lot is for. This comes up often, and the answer is always the same.

If you meet the minimum: subdivisions that meet the precinct minimum are usually assessed as Reconfiguration of a Lot (RC) applications against the scheme's standard codes. Our duty planner can confirm the pathway. For anything beyond the straightforward, think about using a town planning consultant.

If you do not meet the minimum: you can still apply, but the application will be Impact Assessable. That means public notification, and it may be referred to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision instead of being decided by our planning officers. The applicant pays for public notification, and it is up to the applicant to show why the proposal deserves to depart from the scheme's minimum. If you are thinking about this, start with a pre-lodgement meeting ($300, up to 1 hour). See General enquiry vs Pre-Lodgement Meeting — which do I need?

Related: dual occupancies, secondary dwellings and multiple dwellings. If the goal is more housing on the land rather than separate titles, subdivision is not the only option. See Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? or talk through your options with a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Do I need planning approval for a dual occupancy in a residential or rural residential zone?
items.a:
Yes. In the Low density residential, Medium density residential, Rural residential and Township zones, a dual occupancy always needs planning approval (a Material Change of Use). What varies is the pathway, Code or Impact assessment, which depends on the zone, the lot size and the road frontage.

Not sure it is a dual occupancy? First see Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling? In the Rural zone, see Can I build a second house (dual occupancy) on my rural land?

Check your planning zone by searching for the property address on the Online Mapping tool, then go to the section below for your zone.

If your land is in the Low-Density Residential zone

Planning approval is always needed. The only question is which pathway:

  • Code assessable: if the lot is at least 800m².
  • Impact assessable: if the lot is smaller than 800m².

If your land is in the Medium Density Residential zone

Planning approval is always needed, and it is code assessable whatever the lot size.

If your land is in the Rural Residential zone

  • Code assessable: if the lot is at least 8,000m² and has frontage to a constructed road.
  • Impact assessable: if the lot is smaller than 8,000m² or does not have frontage to a constructed road.

If your land is in the Township zone

  • Code assessable: if the lot is at least 1,600m² and has frontage to a constructed sealed road.
  • Impact assessable: if the lot is smaller than 1,600m² or does not have frontage to a constructed sealed road.

Three or more dwellings is different

Three or more dwellings on one lot (flats, units, townhouses, triplexes) is a Multiple Dwellings development, not a dual occupancy, and the rules are different. In short:

  • They are most common in the Low and Medium Density Residential zones, but are also possible in some other zones, such as Township and Mixed Use.
  • There are density caps: one dwelling per 500m² of site area in Low Density, or one per 250m² in Medium Density.
  • For one-bedroom units of 60m² or less, the caps are one per 400m² in Low Density and one per 200m² in Medium Density.
  • Low Density applications are always impact assessable. Medium Density applications are code assessable.

This is a less common question, so talk to a duty planner about your site. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

Things to keep in mind in every zone

  • Overlays can change things. Flood hazard, bushfire hazard, biodiversity, heritage, and Morgan Park / Airport environs overlays can each add requirements. Check the Online Mapping tool.
  • You always need building, plumbing and drainage approvals, separate from planning. The Planning Scheme requirements sit on top of the Building Code of Australia, not in place of it.
  • Typical conditions of approval (where planning approval is needed) cover road works and site access, off-street parking, stormwater discharge, landscaping, buffers from incompatible uses, and infrastructure charges.
  • It stays one title. A dual occupancy approval does not let you sell the dwellings separately. That needs a separate subdivision (Reconfiguring a Lot) approval. If you may want to sell one dwelling one day, see Can I subdivide my land in a residential zone? and talk to a duty planner about which approach suits.
  • A second driveway or new services may need their own approvals. A new access needs a Minor Works Within Road Reserve approval. See Do I need approval for my driveway? on the Building Urban tab. Larger works, such as road upgrades or extended mains, may need operational works approval. See What is operational works, and when do I need approval? A second dwelling can also add bin, water and sewer charges. See How will a dual occupancy or secondary dwelling affect my rates and charges?

The Dual Occupancy (Duplex) in the Residential & Rural Residential Zones fact sheet has the full checklist of acceptable outcomes. For anything that looks borderline, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling?
items.a:
Work this out before anything else. The approvals, the charges and what you can do with the land later are different for each.

  • Secondary dwelling (granny flat): a smaller dwelling used with the main house on the same lot. It is smaller in scale than the house and usually shares its driveway, services, street address and letterbox. It can be attached or free-standing, and it can be rented to anyone.
  • Dual occupancy (duplex): 2 independent dwellings on one lot, attached or detached, for separate households. Each has its own address (for example, 1A and 1B), private open space and parking, and it can have its own services and driveway.

A quick test: if the new dwelling is fully self-contained (kitchen, bathroom, toilet and laundry) and is not smaller than the house and sharing its driveway, services and address, it is likely a dual occupancy, not a secondary dwelling.

Do I need planning approval? It depends on your zone. Find it on the Online Mapping tool.

ZoneDual occupancySecondary dwelling
Low density residentialPlanning approval requiredNot required (unless in the flood hazard overlay)
Medium density residentialPlanning approval requiredNot required (unless in the flood hazard overlay)
Rural residentialPlanning approval requiredPlanning approval required
Township, Mixed usePlanning approval requiredPlanning approval required
RuralMay not be required, if the site meets the checklistPlanning approval required
Whichever it is, and whatever the zone, you always need building approval and plumbing approval. Planning and building are separate approvals from separate teams. See What's the difference between planning approval and building approval?

Read our Dual Occupancy and Secondary Dwellings fact sheet. Its flowchart and comparison table will confirm which one your project is. Then:

  • for a dual occupancy, see Do I need planning approval for a dual occupancy in a residential or rural residential zone? or Can I build a second house (dual occupancy) on my rural land?
  • for a granny flat, see Can I build a granny flat or secondary dwelling? on the Building Urban tab, or Can I build a granny flat (secondary dwelling) on my rural land?

If you are still not sure, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Can I build a second house (dual occupancy) on my rural land?
items.a:
Often, yes, and sometimes without planning approval. In the Rural zone, a dual occupancy does not need planning approval if all 3 of these are true:

  • the lot is at least 10 hectares in area
  • it has frontage to a constructed road, or access to one through a registered easement
  • the proposal meets every item on the Planning Scheme checklist, such as setbacks from boundaries, watercourses and gravel roads, a flood-free building area, distance from animal industries and quarries, and on-site water storage

Work through the checklist in our Dual occupancy (second dwelling) in the Rural Zone fact sheet. If you can tick every item, you skip planning and go straight to building approval (and plumbing approval). See Do I need approval to build on my rural block? on the Building Rural tab.

If you cannot tick everything:

  • If the lot is at least 10 hectares and has constructed road frontage, you need a code-assessable planning application, assessed against the scheme's performance outcomes.
  • If the lot is smaller than 10 hectares, the application is impact-assessable. That means public notification, and the application may be referred to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision. It is worth having a pre-lodgement meeting first. See General enquiry vs Pre-Lodgement Meeting — which do I need?
A granny flat (secondary dwelling) in the Rural zone is different. It always needs planning approval. See Can I build a granny flat (secondary dwelling) on my rural land?

A dual occupancy stays on one title. To create a separate lot, see Can I subdivide my rural land?

Start with the fact sheet checklist. If anything is unclear, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: How will a dual occupancy or secondary dwelling affect my rates and charges?
items.a:
A second dwelling can change your rates notice in several ways:

  • General rates: a property with a dual occupancy (2 dwellings, not strata titled) may be put in the Multi-Residential 1 category, which has a minimum general rate of $2,124 (2026–27). A secondary dwelling does not change your rating category.
  • Bins: in the compulsory waste collection area, each dwelling of a dual occupancy is charged for its own waste and recycling service ($520 a year, 2026–27). For a secondary dwelling, you can ask for an extra bin service. See I don't have a bin service — can I get one? on the Waste tab.
  • Water: the water access charge is per connection. A second water connection means a second access charge ($862 a year in Supply Area 1, 2026–27). Sharing the existing connection does not add one.
  • Sewer: for a dual occupancy, each dwelling pays a sewer charge, even if both share one connection ($888 a year in Warwick and Stanthorpe, 2026–27).
  • Infrastructure charges: a one-off charge is payable with a dual occupancy approval. A secondary dwelling does not attract them.

For how each charge is worked out, see the Rates & Charges Explained page. To check what would apply to your property, call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to a rates officer.

items.q: Can I build a granny flat (secondary dwelling) on my rural land?
items.a:
Yes, but in the Rural zone a secondary dwelling (granny flat) always needs planning approval (a Material Change of Use application), as well as building and plumbing approval. That is different from a dual occupancy, which on a larger rural lot may not need planning approval at all.

To count as a secondary dwelling, it must be used with the main house and be smaller in scale, usually sharing its driveway, services and address. On rural land, "used with" generally means a working connection with the main house. A dwelling built some distance away may not qualify, and may be treated as a dual occupancy instead. A secondary dwelling cannot have its own title or be sold separately.

Check both options. If your lot is at least 10 hectares with constructed road frontage, a second house built as a dual occupancy that meets the Rural zone checklist may not need planning approval. See Can I build a second house (dual occupancy) on my rural land? Which one fits depends on how the dwelling will be used. Compare the two in the Dual Occupancy and Secondary Dwellings fact sheet, or see Is my second dwelling a dual occupancy or a secondary dwelling?

Then talk to a duty planner about your site before you commit to a design. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: What is operational works, and when do I need approval?
items.a:
Operational works is the general term for construction and engineering work that materially affects a property or how it is used, and is not building work or plumbing work. The most common examples are digging out or filling land, and building roads, drainage, or water or sewer infrastructure.

You generally need operational works approval from us when the Southern Downs Planning Scheme makes the work assessable. As a rule of thumb, talk to us first if your project involves:

  • Earthworks: cut or fill more than 1 metre high, or any digging or filling that affects the property or its neighbours.
  • Roads and access: new roads or road upgrades, intersections into a new development, any work on one of our roads (including trenching for services), and footpaths or kerb ramps.
  • Infrastructure: new or extended water, sewer or stormwater mains, and stormwater from a new development that flows beyond the site.
  • Development works: car parks and engineered retaining walls within a development, and the roads, services, lighting and parks that come with a larger subdivision.
  • Land and water: clearing vegetation on freehold land, extracting gravel, sand or soil, forestry, works in a waterway, and works that take or interfere with water under the Water Act 2000.
  • Advertising signs placed on a property.

Building work approved under the Building Act 1975 does not need a separate operational works approval.

Important: it is illegal to change any of our infrastructure without our written approval, even if you have an operational works approval. We do all work on live water and sewer infrastructure.

For the full list, see our Operational Works Application page. If you are not sure whether your work needs approval, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask for the Development Engineer. To apply, see How does an Operational Works application work, and how long does it take?

items.q: How does an Operational Works application work, and how long does it take?
items.a:
These are the steps, with the usual timeframes in step 4:

  1. Get your other approvals first. If the project also needs a Material Change of Use or a Reconfiguration of a Lot, get that approval before you apply for operational works. Its conditions usually shape the operational works design.
  2. Engage an engineer early. The works must be designed and supervised by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ). Your engineer can also lodge the application for you.
  3. Lodge the application on a DA Form 1. Include a cover letter, design drawings (including an erosion and sediment control plan), the RPEQ's design certification, and any reports, such as traffic, flood or stormwater studies. Fees are on our Fees & Charges page.
  4. Assessment. When no information request or State referral is needed, the usual timeline is:
    • we tell you the fees within 10 business days
    • once the fees are paid, we decide within 35 business days
    • the decision notice is issued within a further 5 business days
  5. Before work starts. You pay the rest of the fees and a security deposit, and provide the documents listed in the approval. You also hold a pre-start meeting on site with our development engineer, your engineer and your contractor.
  6. After the work. Your RPEQ certifies the completed works. If the works create assets we will take over, such as roads, mains, drainage or parks, a maintenance period applies, usually 12 months, while we hold a maintenance bond. An off-maintenance inspection follows, and then we return the bond. See the On/Off Maintenance Process page.
An operational works approval usually lapses if the work has not substantially started within 2 years. Your decision notice states the period that applies.

To talk through your project, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask for an appointment with the Development Engineer. For planning applications in general, see How do I make a planning application?

items.q: What approval is required to start a business from my home?
items.a:
Often none. Plenty of small businesses run legitimately from homes in the Southern Downs without any planning approval. The Planning Scheme has a Home-Based Business framework that sets out what can happen at home without a Material Change of Use, and what goes too far and needs one.

Some common examples:

  • Family day care usually fits within the rules. See Can I run a family day care from home?
  • Bed and breakfast fits for up to six guests. See Can I run a bed and breakfast from my home?
  • Mechanic or vehicle repairs are never a home-based business. See Can I run a mechanic or vehicle repair business from home?
  • Food or beauty services also need a licence from us. See Do I need a licence to sell food or offer beauty services from home?

Like short-term accommodation, running a business from home is best thought of as a stack of separate approvals. Even when you do not need planning approval, you often still need other permits. The most common combination is:

  1. Planning approval: only needed if your business goes beyond the Home-Based Business limits (see below).
  2. An industry licence: needed for food businesses and personal appearance services, whatever the planning position. See Do I need a licence to sell food or offer beauty services from home?
  3. Building approval: only if you are physically changing the building or, in rare cases, changing its building classification. See Can I build or convert a building for my home business?

You do not need planning approval if your business stays within all of these limits:

  • Size: up to 40m² of the home in residential zones, or up to 100m² in the Rural zone.
  • Staff: in residential zones, only people who live in the home. In the Rural zone, residents plus one employee who does not live on site.
  • Clients on site: no more than six at any one time, 8am–7pm Monday to Saturday (not public holidays). Family day care has its own rules. See Can I run a family day care from home?
  • Signs: one sign, no bigger than 0.3m², showing only the name, occupation and contact details of the occupier.
  • No retail sales from the premises: mail order and online sales are fine, but no walk-in customers buying goods, no goods on public display and no outside storage.
  • Vehicles: one commercial vehicle for the business (two in the Rural zone). No vehicle over 4.5 tonnes in residential zones. No fuelling, repairing or maintaining vehicles on site (other than cleaning).
  • Not a motor vehicle workshop, medium-impact industry or high-impact industry: these are never a home-based business, whatever their size. See Can I run a mechanic or vehicle repair business from home?

If your business goes beyond any of these limits, it is treated as a Material Change of Use (MCU), which means a planning application. This is more common than people think, and it does not mean we will refuse it. An MCU is simply the pathway that lets us assess the proposal against the Planning Scheme's Performance Outcomes instead of the strict Acceptable Outcomes. Plenty of home businesses that do not fit the standard limits are approved with conditions on hours, parking, signs, notifying neighbours and so on.

If you think your plan might need an MCU, call the duty planner before you commit to anything. General enquiries are free. A 10-minute conversation can shape a proposal so that approval is straightforward.

Other things to know about that we do not manage. You will probably need:

  • an ABN (Australian Business Register)
  • to think about the tax effects of running a business from home (ATO)
  • a working with children check if your business involves children (Blue Card Services)
  • a liquor licence if you plan to serve alcohol (Office of Liquor and Gaming Regulation)
  • WorkCover if you employ staff

Business Queensland (business.qld.gov.au) has good checklists for each.

The full Home-Based Business rules are in section 9.3.4 of the Southern Downs Planning Scheme. For anything that looks borderline, or to discuss whether an MCU is the right path for your business, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

items.q: Can I run a mechanic or vehicle repair business from home?
items.a:
No. Vehicle servicing and repair, motor vehicle workshops, shops, warehouses and transport depots are not home-based businesses under the Planning Scheme. Fuelling, servicing or repairing vehicles on site is not allowed as part of one.

A business like this needs its own planning approval as a different use, and the Planning Scheme decides which zones it can go in. Talk to a duty planner before you sign a lease or buy equipment. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: Can I run a family day care from home?
items.a:
Usually without planning approval. Family day care (minding children under school age in your home) is a home-based business under the Planning Scheme. It does not need planning approval if it meets the home-based business rules, including:

  • no more than six children being minded at any one time
  • in residential zones, only people who live in the home work in the business. In the Rural zone, up to one employee who does not live there
  • one sign up to 0.3m², and no outside storage

The usual home business hours (8am–7pm Monday to Saturday) and floor area limit do not apply to family day care. For the other rules, see What approval is required to start a business from my home?

Planning is only one part. Family day care has its own registration and care regulations, which we do not manage. Check what applies to you before you start.

To check your plans against the planning rules, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. General enquiries are free.

items.q: What approvals are necessary for a farm stand?
Do I need a licence to sell food or offer beauty services from home?
items.a:
Yes, for some businesses. You need these licences whether or not your business needs planning approval.

  • Food businesses: if you make or sell food as part of your business (baked goods, meals, catering, market stalls, mobile coffee, home kitchens), you need a separate Food Business Licence under the Food Act 2006. See Food Businesses.
  • Personal Appearance Services: higher-risk services, such as tattooing, body piercing and other skin penetration procedures, need a licence under the Public Health (Infection Control for Personal Appearance Services) Act 2003, wherever they are done. Lower-risk services, such as hairdressing and beauty therapy, do not need a licence but must still meet infection control requirements. See Personal Appearance Services.

You must get the licence before you start trading, and renew it every year. For other types of business, see What approval is required to start a business from my home?

items.q: Can I build or convert a building for my home business?
items.a:
Usually not without a planning application. A home-based business has to stay secondary to the home. Building a new structure for it, or reclassifying a building (especially to a commercial class 2–9), usually takes it outside the home-based business definition. You would then need a planning application.

Using part of your house or shed may still mean reclassifying that part for building purposes, unless it is less than 10% of the floor area of that storey. Every bed and breakfast needs a change of classification to Class 1b.

The details are in our Home-Based Business fact sheet. To check what your building needs, call our building team on 1300 697 372 or ask your private certifier.

items.q: How do I check on the status of a planning application?
items.a:
For your own application, contact the planning officer handling it. Email is usually easiest, or call 1300 697 372 to be put through. If the officer is not available, Customer Service can take your details and arrange a call back.

For applications that are not yours, the Application Tracking Tool and the Online Mapping tool together cover most of what is publicly available. Some information is held back from people who are not the applicant, for privacy reasons.

Our Application Tracking Tool lets you check the public information on any planning application in the Southern Downs region. It shows the lodgement date, current stage and decision status of every application since 2010.

People most often use the tracking tool to look up:

  • a neighbour's application, especially for housing estates, subdivisions or commercial developments nearby, to understand what is proposed before deciding whether to make a submission
  • a property you are thinking of buying, to check whether any current or recent applications affect the land

items.q: I can't find an application in the Application Tracking Tool. What am I doing wrong?
items.a:
Usually nothing. It is the search, not you. The Application Tracking Tool works best with a broader search, not a fuller one.

  • Search by suburb or application number wherever you can.
  • Avoid searching by full street address. Exact addresses often return nothing, even when they are correct.
  • Fill in as few fields as possible. Adding more fields, even correct ones, makes a match less likely, not more.
If a search by suburb returns a long list, sort or scan it rather than adding fields to shorten it. Still stuck? Call 1300 697 372.

items.q: Can I talk to my Councillor about a development application?
items.a:
Yes, you can contact your Councillor, but there are rules about what they can say and how those conversations happen. The rules are in our Planning Protocols Policy (PL-142), which makes sure planning decisions are made fairly and openly.

Councillors do not decide most applications. Council has delegated the power to decide development applications to the Chief Executive Officer, and our planning officers decide most of them. The Chief Executive Officer, a General Manager or the Manager can refer an application to an Ordinary Council meeting for decision.

What a Councillor can do

  • Give general information about the application process, but not advice on whether an application is likely to be approved.
  • Talk about what is already publicly known about an application.
  • Suggest you get independent advice, such as from a planning consultant, or, if you are planning to lodge an application, book a pre-lodgement meeting with our planners.

Once an application is lodged

  • Any opinion a Councillor gives is their personal view. It does not represent Council's position on the application.
  • A meeting with a Councillor to discuss the issues in an application must be arranged through the Chief Executive Officer's office, with one of our officers present.
  • Councillors keep a written record of conversations about development applications, and it goes on our records.
  • Talking to or emailing a Councillor is not a submission. If you want your view considered in the decision, and to keep your appeal rights, make a properly made submission to us during the public notification period. See How do I object to a planning application near me?
  • If an application is going to an Ordinary Council meeting, Councillors will not accept lobbying or new submissions in the 48 hours before the meeting. New material at that stage can mean the item is deferred to a later meeting.
  • Councillors will not discuss a decision with the applicant or submitters while it can still be appealed, or while it is before the Planning & Environment Court.

Lobbyists acting for someone else must tell a Councillor they are a lobbyist when they first make contact. The contact is recorded in our Register of Contact with Lobbyists.

For questions about a particular application, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. You can also write to us at mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: How do I object to a planning application near me?
items.a:
Make a properly made submission during the public notification period. Only Impact Assessment applications go through public notification, so you can only make a submission while one is open. If the application is under Code Assessment, there is no public submission process. We assess it against the codes without public input.

A properly made submission makes sure your objection is considered in the decision and keeps your right of appeal. It must:

  • be in writing and signed by each person making the submission
  • be received during the public notification period (usually 15 business days; check the dates on the site sign or in the newspaper notice)
  • include the name and address of every submitter
  • include one (1) postal or email address for all the submitters
  • include the grounds of the submission, and the facts and circumstances you are relying on to support those grounds
  • be addressed to the assessment manager: Southern Downs Regional Council

The simplest way to lodge it is by email to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. Our Development Applications requiring Public Notification page has more about the process.

Talking to or emailing a Councillor is not a submission. If you want your view considered in the decision, and to keep your appeal rights, send us a properly made submission within the notification period.

Grounds that carry weight relate to the Planning Scheme: effects on traffic, noise, amenity, hours of operation, overshadowing, the character of the area, stormwater, environmental values and similar. Personal or commercial grievances (disliking the applicant, competing with the proposed business, a drop in property value) generally do not carry weight in planning terms. We have to assess the application against the scheme, not against commercial or personal interests.

Every properly made submitter receives a copy of the Decision Notice, whatever the decision. If the application is approved, properly made submitters have a right of appeal to the Planning & Environment Court.

If the application goes to a Council meeting. Our planning officers decide most applications under delegation, but some are referred to an Ordinary Council meeting. If that happens, we will tell submitters the meeting date at least 48 hours beforehand, and you can ask to address Councillors at a Councillor Information Session. Councillors will not accept lobbying or new submissions in the 48 hours before the meeting. New material at that stage can mean the item is deferred to a later meeting.

If you are not sure whether an application is code or impact assessable, or how to word a submission, talk to a duty planner. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. We cannot tell you what to say in a submission, as that would not be appropriate. But we can explain the process, the timeframes, and what the scheme considers relevant.

items.q: Who decides on wind farms and large-scale solar farms?
items.a:
The State Government, not us. Since July 2025, under the Planning (Social Impact and Community Benefit) and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2025, the State Assessment and Referral Agency (SARA) assesses and decides wind farms and large-scale solar farms. We cannot approve or refuse them.

The process for these projects is:

  1. The developer prepares a Social Impact Assessment. This is a report on how the project will affect the community, good and bad, including consultation with residents, landholders and businesses.
  2. We review the Social Impact Assessment and negotiate a Community Benefit Agreement with the developer. This is a legally binding agreement setting out what the community gets for hosting the project. It must be in place before the developer can lodge an application.
  3. The developer lodges the application with the State. These projects are impact assessable, so the application is publicly notified and anyone can make a submission for or against it.
  4. The State assesses the application and makes the final decision.

If a project is approved, we monitor that the benefits in the Community Benefit Agreement are delivered. The whole process can take from many months to several years.

To have your say on a particular project, make a submission to the State during its public notification period. The notice will say how.

Our Renewable Energy and Community Benefits page has more, including our Renewable Energy Community Benefit System Policy and free advice services for landholders approached by developers. For other questions, write to us at mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au.
