tabs.label: Animals
tabs.intro: Animal management in the Southern Downs covers a lot of ground — registering your dog, keeping the right number of pets for your property, dealing with a barking neighbour, and what to do when you find a stray, an injured kangaroo, or your dog wandering off. This page works through the most common questions in four sections: pets at home, lost/found/impounded animals, nuisance and safety, and dog breeding. For anything not covered here, Council's Local Laws Team can be reached on 1300 697 372.

items.q: How do I register my dog?
items.a:
Fill in the Dog Registration Application. Then post it, email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au, or bring it to one of our Customer Service Centres. If you post or email it and want to pay by card, include a phone number and we will call you for your card details.

All dogs in the Southern Downs must be registered under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008. This means:

  • All dogs must be registered from 12 weeks of age.
  • All animals new to the region must be registered within 14 days of arriving.
  • Animals must be microchipped from 12 weeks of age.
  • Only working dogs do not have to be registered and microchipped. See our Working Dogs page, or I'm a primary producer with working dogs. Do the breeder rules apply to me?
  • We recommend desexing at an appropriate age.

Fees (registration runs for the calendar year):

StandardPensioner
Desexed$45$40
Not desexed$170$150
  • Puppies under 6 months pay the desexed rate.
  • Registered assistance dogs: no fee.
  • Renewals paid within 30 days of the renewal notice get 10% off.
  • A dog registered after 1 October is registered until 31 December the following year.
  • Owners can only get one reduction per dog.

Full details are on our Dog Registration page. For questions, call our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: Do I need to register my cat?
items.a:
No. You do not need to register cats with us in the Southern Downs. But under Queensland law (the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008), cats over 12 weeks of age must be microchipped, even if they only live indoors.

The number of cats you can keep without a permit depends on where you live. See How many animals am I allowed to keep on my property? If you breed cats, there are separate rules. See I'd like to breed cats. What permits do I need?

items.q: How many animals am I allowed to keep on my property?
items.a:
It depends on your zone, the size of your lot and the type of animal. The limits are set by our Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) and the Planning Scheme.

Cats (over 3 months old: kittens under 3 months do not count towards the limit):

  • Aerodrome precinct (Massie or Applethorpe): 0 cats (no animals at all are allowed in these precincts)
  • Multi-residential premises: 1 cat
  • Designated town area, lot under 2,000m²: 2 cats
  • Designated town area, lot 2,000m² or more: 3 cats
  • Outside designated town areas: 4 cats

Dogs (over 3 months old): the number you can keep without approval depends on the size of the lot.

LotDogs without approval
Aerodrome precinct (Massie or Applethorpe)0
Under 450m²1
450m² to under 2,000m²2
2,000m² to under 2 hectares3
2 hectares or more4

With approval, you can keep one extra dog on a lot under 2 hectares, or up to 10 dogs on 2 hectares or more. Working dogs cannot be kept in a designated town area. Details are in the Keeping of Dogs fact sheet.

Other animals: limits depend on your zone, lot size and the type of animal. The full list is in the Keeping of Animals Fact Sheet.

To keep more animals than the standard limits, you need a Permit for Keeping of Animals under Subordinate Local Law No. 1.5. Permits last 12 months and must be renewed every year. Conditions usually include desexing, not causing a nuisance to neighbours, and a clean enclosure. Cat breeders can apply for an Animal Breeder Permit for up to 4 breeding cats. See I'd like to breed cats. What permits do I need?

Call us on 1300 697 372 to discuss your situation before you apply.

items.q: How many animals can I keep on a rural block?
items.a:
Rural land generally allows more types and numbers of animals than residential land. Horses, cattle, sheep, goats, alpacas and poultry are all typical. There are still limits, though. They depend on the type of animal, your lot size and your zone.

The Keeping of Animals Fact Sheet sets out the numbers allowed by animal type and zone. It is the definitive source. It covers everything from dogs and cats to horses, cattle, poultry, bees, pigs and exotic animals, with the most you can keep of each without a permit.

If you want to keep more than the standard number, you need a Keeping of Animals permit. Call us on 1300 697 372 before you apply. Our Local Laws team can tell you whether a permit is likely to be approved for your block.

Some breeds and species are restricted or prohibited whatever the size of your lot (restricted breed dogs, some reptiles, feral animals). Check the fact sheet before buying, breeding or moving animals to a new property.

items.q: Can I adopt a dog or cat from Council?
items.a:
Adoptions are usually handled by Southern Downs ARK, a local volunteer-run organisation that works with us to rehome impounded and surrendered animals. ARK takes most animals from our pound, has them vet-checked, vaccinated, microchipped and desexed, and then matches them with new homes. They are the best place to start if you want to adopt.

Visit Southern Downs ARK to see the animals available, adoption fees and how to apply.

In rare cases, you may be able to adopt a particular animal at our pound directly through us. Call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to a Local Laws Officer. This is uncommon, but it is possible if the circumstances suit.

items.q: Can I surrender my pet?
items.a:
Yes. We accept surrendered dogs and cats. But surrendering your pet to Southern Downs ARK directly is often easier for the animal. ARK can start rehoming it straight away, instead of the animal going through the pound first. Visit Southern Downs ARK to find out more.

If you choose to surrender your pet to us:

  • You pay a surrender fee. See our Fees & Charges page for the current fee.
  • Fill in the Owners Request to Privately Impound Dog/Cat form. You can get it from our Customer Service Centres or by calling 1300 697 372.
  • You will need to give details about the animal (breed, age, colour, microchip number, registration and vaccinations) and the reason you are surrendering it.
  • We may refuse a surrender, especially for injured or seriously ill animals. In those cases, contact a vet first.

Once surrendered, the animal becomes our responsibility, and we may transfer it to ARK for rehoming.

Feral or pest animals on your property, such as wild dogs, feral cats, foxes or feral pigs, cannot be surrendered. See the Pest Animals tab for how to manage them.

items.q: My dog is missing or has been impounded. What do I do?
items.a:
Call us as soon as possible on 1300 697 372. Tell us your dog's breed, colour, size and tag number.

If your dog has been impounded, a Local Laws Officer will tell you when you can collect it, the release fee, and whether it must be registered before release. If it has not been impounded, we will add your dog's details to our lost and found register, to help reunite you once it is found.

You can also check the Impounded and Rescued Animals page.

items.q: Where are the Council pound facilities?
items.a:
We run 2 pounds in the Southern Downs region:

  • Warwick Pound: 113 Wentworth Street, Warwick QLD 4370
  • Stanthorpe Pound: 26270 New England Highway, Stanthorpe QLD 4380

Hours and contact details for each pound are on our Pound Facilities page. Before you go, call us on 1300 697 372 to check your animal is at the pound and to arrange to pay any fees.

items.q: I've found a stray dog. What should I do?
items.a:
Call us on 1300 697 372. A Local Laws Officer will come and collect the dog.

Do not try to hold or restrain a dog you do not know. Even a friendly dog can bite when stressed.

items.q: There's livestock on the road. Who do I call?
items.a:
For animals on our roads, call 1300 697 372. Our Local Laws Officers treat livestock on roads as a priority because of the risk to drivers.

If the animal is on a highway, call the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) on 13 19 40. TMR is better equipped to deal with highway hazards safely.

Have this information ready when you call to help us respond:

  • the closest street address or landmark, and which way the animal is heading
  • the type of animal (cattle, horse, sheep, goat) and roughly how many
  • the breed or colour, if you can tell
  • whether the animal looks injured or distressed

If it is an immediate hazard, such as animals on a major road at night or after a crash, call 000 first, then tell us.

items.q: I've found injured wildlife, or there's a snake or possum in the house. What do I do?
items.a:
We do not attend wildlife callouts. Specialist volunteer organisations, licensed under Queensland's wildlife management rules, handle wildlife rescue. We can give you information and point you to the right service.

For injured wildlife (such as kangaroos, koalas, birds or possums hit by a car or hurt in some other way): see our Caring for Wildlife page. It has current rescue group contacts and what to do while you wait. After a flood, fire, storm or other emergency, start with the Help After a Disaster — Wildlife page.

For snakes and possums in homes: our Possums and Snakes page lists licensed snake catchers and possum removal contacts in the region. Do not try to handle a snake yourself. Even non-venomous snakes can give a painful bite, and getting the species wrong is dangerous.

items.q: My neighbour's dog barks constantly. Can Council do something?
items.a:
Yes. Barking that keeps happening is a noise nuisance we can investigate under our local laws. The process works in steps:

  1. Talk to the owner first. Often they do not know. A friendly note often sorts it out without us getting involved.
  2. Lodge a service request using our online service request form or by calling 1300 697 372.
  3. Keep a noise diary. We will ask you to record dates, times and how the barking affects you. This is essential. Without it, we have limited power to act.
  4. We investigate. Once we receive the diary, a Local Laws Officer will contact the dog's owner.
Download the Barking Dogs Fact Sheet and Noise Diary to get started.

items.q: Why does Council need a noise diary? Why can't an officer just come and listen?
items.a:
Our Local Laws Officers start investigating as soon as we receive a noise complaint. But to prove a genuine nuisance under the law, they need to show a pattern. The barking dog diary gives them an objective record of that pattern. It also protects you by recording the problem factually.

The diary comes with our Barking Dogs fact sheet. To make a complaint, see My neighbour's dog barks constantly. Can Council do something?

items.q: I've been told my dog barks when I'm away. What are my options?
items.a:
Most barking that keeps happening has a cause, such as boredom, separation anxiety, territorial stress, not enough exercise, or something nearby the dog is reacting to. Dealing with the cause usually works better than trying to stop the barking itself.

Things to try first:

  • more exercise
  • toys that keep the dog busy
  • a secure, shaded place to rest
  • where possible, blocking the dog's view of things that set it off

As a short-term way to change the behaviour, you can also hire a barking collar from us. Hire is $16 per week or part of a week, with a $100 refundable deposit. You must claim the deposit back within 3 months of returning the collar, or you will not get it back.

How to hire: fill in the Application for Hire of Cat/Fox Trap or Barking Collar or Tree Pear Injector form. Bring it, with proof of identity (driver's licence, passport or other accepted ID), to our Warwick, Stanthorpe or Allora Customer Service Centre.

Prices are current as of April 2026 and may change. See our current Fees & Charges schedule for any updates.

If the barking continues despite your reasonable efforts, talk to your vet or an animal behaviourist. A medical problem (pain, or mental decline in older dogs) or severe separation anxiety may need professional help rather than equipment.

items.q: I've been attacked by a dog. What do I do?
items.a:
If anyone needs emergency medical help, call 000 first.

Once you are safe, call us on 1300 697 372 to record the details of the attack. If needed, a Local Laws Officer will come to the scene.

When you call, have ready:

  • the location
  • a description of the dog
  • whether it is still in the area
  • the time of the attack

You will also need to fill in a Statement of Dog Attack form and email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

items.q: I'm thinking of breeding my dog. What do I need to do?
items.a:
If you breed a dog (born on or after 26 May 2017), you must register as a breeder with the Queensland Dog Breeder Register. You must also get a supply number, which goes into the puppy's microchip information. This applies even if:

  • you are a casual or "mum and dad" breeder
  • the litter was unplanned or accidental
  • you are only giving puppies to family or friends

Dog breeding in Queensland is covered by state law: the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008, run by Biosecurity Queensland. We support the system, but we do not run it.

The narrow exemption is for primary producers on rural land breeding working dogs for other primary producers to use as working dogs. See I'm a primary producer with working dogs. Do the breeder rules apply to me? for the legal definition.

What to do, in order:

  • Register online at the Queensland Dog Breeder Register. It is free and quick. You will get a Breeder Identification Number (your "supply number"), which lasts 12 months and can be renewed every year.
  • You must register within 28 days of a litter being born.
  • When the puppies are microchipped (which state law requires), the person implanting the chip must include your supply number in the chip information.
  • When you sell, give away or advertise a puppy, you must show the supply number in the advertisement and give it to the new owner.

There are penalties for selling or giving away a puppy without a supply number. They apply to the breeder and to any pet shop or third party that sells the puppy on without proper documents.

Found dogs and one-off cases: you may be able to get a Breeder Exemption Number instead if you have found a dog you want to rehome (rather than surrendering it to us), or you are not a business and are rehoming a dog you did not breed. Apply through the same Queensland Dog Breeder Register portal.

We cannot register breeders or issue supply numbers. For those questions, contact Biosecurity Queensland on 13 25 23 or visit qdbr.dpi.qld.gov.au.

items.q: I'm a primary producer with working dogs. Do the breeder rules apply to me?
items.a:
Mostly no, but with important conditions. Working dog breeders do not have to register, but the exemption is narrower than many landholders think.

Under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008, a working dog is a dog usually kept (or to be kept) on rural land by an owner who is a primary producer (or someone employed by a primary producer). It must be kept mainly for droving, protecting, tending or working stock, or being trained to do so.

Pig dogs are NOT working dogs under the Act. The legal definition only covers dogs that work stock. Managing feral animals does not count.

The exemption only applies when all of these are true:

  • you are a primary producer breeding on rural land
  • all the puppies go to other primary producers
  • those puppies will be kept on rural land as working dogs

If any puppy from the litter goes anywhere else (sold to someone who is not a primary producer, kept as a pet, given to a friend in town), you must register as a breeder for that puppy and give a supply number.

Selling a working dog you did not breed to someone who is not a primary producer, or who will not use it as a working dog, needs a Breeder Exemption Number for that dog, even though you are a primary producer. Apply through the Queensland Dog Breeder Register. You need a separate exemption number for each dog.

If in doubt, register. It is free, takes minutes, and avoids penalties.

items.q: I'd like to breed cats. What permits do I need?
items.a:
It depends how many breeding cats you keep. Cat breeding is covered by both state law (microchipping under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008) and our local laws and Planning Scheme, which cover keeping breeding cats.

Up to 4 breeding cats: Animal Breeder Permit (from us)

If you want to keep more cats than the standard limits (see How many animals am I allowed to keep on my property?), you can apply to us for an Animal Breeder Permit for up to 4 breeding cats. To apply, you will need:

  • the completed application form
  • plans and details of the cats' enclosure
  • the application fee (see Fees & Charges)
  • written evidence that you belong to a recognised cat breeder association, and that all your breeding cats are registered with it

More than 4 breeding cats: planning approval (Animal Keeping)

For more than 4 breeding cats, you need an "Animal keeping" application under the Planning Scheme:

  • Rural zone, lot of at least 20 hectares, fewer than 10 cats: Code assessable
  • All other situations: Impact assessable (public notification required)

The Planning tab explains what code assessable and impact assessable mean in practice.

A duty planner can talk through your situation before you commit to an application. Lodge an online service request under Planning enquiry and a duty planner will get back to you within 5 business days. Or call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

Note: the microchipping rules for cats apply whether or not you are a breeder. Every cat you supply must be microchipped before it leaves your care.

items.q: What's my legal responsibility for pest animals on my property?
items.a:
Every landholder in Queensland has a general biosecurity obligation (GBO) under the Biosecurity Act 2014, the same law that covers weeds. Put simply, if an invasive animal is on your land and there are reasonable, practical steps you could take to limit its damage or spread, you are expected to take them.

General Biosecurity Obligation (GBO): Take all reasonable and practical measures to minimise the biosecurity risk posed by invasive animals under your control. What counts as "reasonable and practical" depends on your situation (a small lifestyle block, a large grazing property, or a suburban home), so there is no single checklist that fits everyone.

Several species are also formally declared restricted invasive animals. This means they must not be moved, kept, fed, given away, sold or released. For Southern Downs landholders, the ones that come up most often are:

  • wild dog and dingo (Canis familiaris / Canis familiaris dingo)
  • European red fox (Vulpes vulpes)
  • feral pig (Sus scrofa)
  • feral cat (Felis catus), meaning a cat with no owner
  • rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), both wild and domestic
  • feral deer, mainly fallow deer (Dama dama) in the Southern Downs

Indian mynas and some other urban pests are not declared restricted species. They are still covered by the GBO, and landholders can manage them. See Indian mynas are nesting in my roof or making a mess. What can I do?

For the official species list and control advice, see the Queensland Government — Invasive animals page. For advice about your property, call our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: Wild dogs are attacking my stock. What should I do?
items.a:
Wild dogs (including dingoes, dingo crosses and roaming domestic dogs with no owner) are one of the biggest pest animal problems for producers in the Southern Downs. If they are attacking your stock:

  1. Protect the stock you have left. If you can, move vulnerable animals, such as lambing ewes, calving cows and young stock, to paddocks closer to the house or into yards.
  2. Record the evidence. Photograph carcasses, bite patterns, tracks and droppings before you move or get rid of anything. Note GPS locations if you can. This helps officers assess the situation and supports coordinated control.
  3. Report it to us and log it in FeralScan. Call 1300 697 372 or use the MySDRC online service request. In the free FeralScan app (WildDogScan), you can log sightings, attacks and control work. The data helps us and your neighbours work together.
  4. Talk to your neighbours. Wild dogs roam over large areas. Control on one property alone rarely lasts long, because dogs from surrounding country quickly fill the gap. Working together across neighbouring properties is the most effective thing you can do.

Control methods available to landholders include:

  • 1080 baiting: the cheapest option over large areas. See Does Council run a 1080 baiting program? How do I get baits?
  • trapping with padded foot-hold traps
  • shooting
  • exclusion fencing, including cluster fencing with your neighbours
  • livestock guardian animals, such as maremma dogs and alpacas. Some producers use these successfully, but they need careful planning if trapping or baiting is also happening nearby.

Our Local Laws Team can advise which mix of methods suits your property, and help put you in touch with neighbouring landholders for joint programs. Call 1300 697 372.

items.q: How does Council's Wild Dog Bounty work?
items.a:
We pay a bounty on wild dogs destroyed in the Southern Downs region, to encourage ongoing control. Current payments are:

  • $50 per pup (up to 14 weeks of age)
  • $100 per wild dog (over 14 weeks of age)

How to claim:

  1. Destroy the dog within the Southern Downs Regional Council area.
  2. Log the kill in FeralScan. The claim form asks for this.
  3. Bring the whole dog (not just a scalp) to one of our Authorised Persons within 60 days of destroying it.
  4. Fill in the Claim for Wild Dog Bounty form. The Authorised Person signs it to confirm they received the dog and made it unusable for future claims.
  5. If you have not claimed a bounty from us in the last 2 years, include a completed SDRC Electronic Transfer Form. If you do not have an ABN, also include an ABS Statement by Supplier form.
The bounty is meant to support other control methods, such as coordinated baiting, exclusion fencing and guardian animals, not replace them. Bounty payments are a privilege, not a legal right, and we can change them.

Contact our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372 to confirm current rates and arrange a time to bring dogs to an Authorised Person.

items.q: Can I hire traps from Council for feral cats or foxes?
items.a:
Yes. Residents can hire wire cage traps from us to deal with feral cats, stray cats or foxes on their property. Traps are in high demand, so call ahead to check one is available.

How to hire: fill in the Application for Hire of Cat/Fox Trap or Barking Collar or Tree Pear Injector form. Bring it, with proof of identity (driver's licence, passport or other accepted ID), to our Warwick, Stanthorpe or Allora Customer Service Centre. You hire a trap for one week.

Fees. Hire is $16 per week or part of a week, with a $100 refundable deposit. You must claim the deposit back within 3 months of returning the trap, or you will not get it back. Prices are current as of April 2026 and may change. See our current Fees & Charges schedule for any updates.

Using the trap safely:

  • Check the trap at least twice a day: first thing in the morning and again in the late afternoon.
  • Never leave a baited, set trap unattended for more than 12 hours.
  • Keep the trap out of direct sun, and give shade and water if it has to stay set overnight.
  • Release any other animals you catch (possums, native birds, pet cats) straight away and unharmed.

Drop-off: you can bring cats you catch to our Animal Control Officers at the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound. Or put them in the 24-hour drop-off boxes at either pound, which we check every day, including weekends and public holidays. For foxes, call us before you drop off.

Our Local Laws Team can also advise on where to put the trap, what bait to use, and animal welfare. Call 1300 697 372.

items.q: Does Council run a 1080 baiting program? How do I get baits?
items.a:
Yes. We are an authorised supplier of 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate) baits for wild dog and fox control. Landholders have 2 options:

  1. Buy ready-made baits from us. These are currently $38 for a 10-pack of wild dog baits (April 2026, may change). You can pick them up from the Warwick and Stanthorpe pounds.
  2. Bring your own fresh meat to the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound, and we will inject it with 1080. Many landholders prefer this, because wild dogs in an area may already be used to taking a particular meat from that property.

Before you bait, you must:

  • attend a baiting briefing or sign the required acknowledgements (we will guide you through this)
  • tell all neighbours next to your property at least 72 hours beforehand
  • put up warning signs at every entrance to your property before baiting starts, and leave them up for at least one month afterwards
  • keep working dogs muzzled or restrained, and move livestock out of baited paddocks as the product label says
1080 is extremely toxic to dogs and there is no reliable antidote. Baits and poisoned carcasses stay toxic for a long time. If your working dog or family pet takes a bait or eats a poisoned animal, it usually dies. Telling neighbours, putting up signs and placing baits correctly are legal requirements, not guidelines.

Timing: many landholders bait twice a year: usually March–May (targeting breeding adults) and again in September–November (targeting pups and young dogs). Results improve greatly when you and your neighbours put baits out at about the same time.

Call our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372 to arrange baits, or to discuss whether baiting is right for your situation.

items.q: I've got feral pig damage on my property. What can I do?
items.a:
Feral pigs are a restricted invasive animal. They must not be kept, fed or moved. On rural properties, the common signs are rooted-up pasture and crops, wallows near water, damaged fences, and lambs or poultry going missing.

Control options that work:

  • Trapping with a pig-specific trigger is the easiest method for small and medium properties. Silo-style cage traps with a funnel entrance or a lift-bar trigger are selective: only pigs set them off. Feeding the pigs for several nights before you set the trigger greatly improves how many you catch.
  • 1080 baiting is the most effective option over large areas. It has the same rules on telling neighbours, signs and pre-feeding as wild dog baiting. Fermented grain is a common and effective bait.
  • Fencing with sheep mesh held tight to the ground, ideally with an electrified offset wire, can protect high-value crops or small paddocks.
  • Shooting from the ground or the air can work where there are fewer pigs or in open country. Thermal imaging helps find them at night.

You can hire a Hog Hopper from us. This is a bait station with a weighted, hinged lid. Pigs can lift it with their snouts, but native animals, kangaroos and wallabies, and most livestock cannot. It makes 1080 pig baiting much safer for other animals, and is especially useful on properties with wildlife corridors or mixed grazing.

  • Hire is free, with a $100 refundable deposit.
  • The longest hire period is 2 weeks.
  • You can claim the deposit back within 3 months of returning it.

Call 1300 697 372 to arrange it.

Pigs roam over large areas and breed quickly, so a control program on one property alone is rarely enough. Work with your neighbours whenever you can.

Feral pigs can carry diseases that people can catch, including leptospirosis, brucellosis, Q fever and melioidosis. Wear gloves and avoid touching blood, urine or faeces. Do not eat undercooked feral pig meat. Do not feed raw feral pig meat or offal to dogs, because swine brucellosis can pass from pigs to dogs to people.

Our Local Laws Team can discuss trap designs, arrange baits, and help coordinate control across neighbouring properties. Call 1300 697 372.

items.q: I've got a rabbit problem. What should I do?
items.a:
If you see a wild rabbit in the Southern Downs, report it quickly to the Darling Downs-Moreton Rabbit Board (DDMRB) on 07 4661 4076 or to us on 1300 697 372. The DDMRB has specialist officers for rabbit control in the protected zone.

Queensland is the only Australian state with a rabbit-free zone. It is protected by a rabbit-proof fence and actively managed by the DDMRB. The Southern Downs is inside this zone, which is why we treat rabbit sightings here seriously.

Pet rabbits are illegal in Queensland. Domestic and wild rabbits are the same species and will interbreed if domestic rabbits escape. You cannot keep a pet rabbit, even a desexed one in a secure hutch. Permits are only issued for research or some forms of public entertainment (for example, magic shows and circuses).

If you have a pet rabbit now, do not release it into the wild. You can:

  • surrender it to us at our Warwick or Stanthorpe office
  • contact the Darling Downs-Moreton Rabbit Board on 07 4661 4076 to arrange collection
  • arrange for a vet to put it down humanely

We and the DDMRB would much rather help you sort out a pet rabbit than see one released. Get in touch, and no one will give you a hard time about it.

items.q: Are feral deer a problem in the Southern Downs?
items.a:
Yes. The Southern Downs is home to the largest wild fallow deer herd in Queensland, centred on the Pikedale area south-west of Warwick. For most landholders in the region, deer are a quiet background fact of rural life rather than a pressing problem. But if they are damaging crops, pasture or fences on your property, the following applies.

Fallow deer were first released on the Darling Downs around Westbrook and Warwick between 1870 and 1872. The Pikedale herd now runs on into the large New England Tableland population across the NSW border.

Species. Fallow deer (Dama dama) are the species to know locally. Queensland also has established herds of red, chital and rusa deer, but those are well north and east of the Southern Downs.

Legal status. Feral fallow deer are a category 3, 4 and 6 restricted invasive animal under the Biosecurity Act 2014. They must not be moved, fed, given away, sold or released. The same general biosecurity obligation (GBO) that applies to other invasive animals applies here: take reasonable and practical steps to minimise the biosecurity risk on land you control.

Farmed deer and deer in game parks are treated separately and must be kept in deer-proof enclosures. If an enclosed deer escapes and establishes in the wild, the owner is responsible under the Act. Anyone keeping deer must register as a biosecurity entity.

Control options for landholders:

  • Shooting from the ground is considered the most effective and humane method available. It is usually done at night from a vehicle with spotlights or thermal equipment, by trained people with the right firearms licences.
  • Shooting from a helicopter can be cost-effective on large or open properties. It is a specialised operation, best coordinated across several neighbouring landholders.
  • Trapping is sometimes an option on the edges of towns, where shooting is not practical. This is usually a self-closing gate set off by a trip wire, or a clover trap. Traps must be checked often, and animals promptly tranquilised or put down. Animal welfare is a serious consideration.
  • Exclusion fencing works but is expensive. A proper deer fence is about 2.1m high, with heavy-duty strainers, posts 9m apart, and netting pegged to the ground. It is usually only practical for protecting high-value crops or farmed enclosures, not whole properties.
  • Using licensed recreational hunters is common among local landholders. Think about access conditions, public liability insurance and references before you let anyone onto your property.

Working together matters. Deer roam over large areas and move freely between properties. Control on one property is usually undone by deer moving in from surrounding country. Joint effort across several neighbouring landholders works much better than anyone working alone. Our Local Laws Team and local Landcare groups can help put landholders dealing with the same problem in touch.

For help identifying species, detailed control advice and the Queensland Feral Deer Management Strategy 2022–27, see Biosecurity Queensland — Invasive animals. To discuss deer on your property or in your area, call our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: My neighbour's cat keeps coming onto my property. What are my options?
items.a:
Start with a friendly conversation with the cat's owner. Roaming cats are a common nuisance complaint. Often the owner does not realise the cat is causing a problem, and a calm chat sorts it out without us getting involved.

If you cannot talk to the owner, or talking does not help:

  1. Hire a cat trap from us. They are often used for exactly this. Call ahead to check one is available. See Can I hire traps from Council for feral cats or foxes?
  2. Bring the cat you catch to the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound. There are 24-hour drop-off boxes, which we check every day, including weekends and public holidays.
  3. If the cat is microchipped, we will try to contact the owner. We hold cats with a microchip that identifies an owner for at least 5 days. We hold cats with no ID for at least 3 days. After that, we assess them for rehoming (often through Southern Downs Ark) or decide what else to do with them.
We run a subsidised cat desexing and microchipping program through the National Desexing Network, depending on the funding available each year. Desexed cats are less likely to roam or fight, and a current microchip is the best way to make sure a lost cat comes home. Call 1300 697 372 to check who is eligible and whether places are available.

items.q: Indian mynas are nesting in my roof or making a mess. What can I do?
items.a:
Indian mynas are not a declared restricted species, but they are still covered by the general biosecurity obligation, and we support residents who want to control them. They compete aggressively for tree hollows and push out native parrots. Nests in roofs can bring mites, lice and a fire risk.

Do not confuse Indian mynas with native noisy miners. They look alike at first glance, but noisy miners are native and protected. To tell them apart: Indian mynas have a brown body and bright yellow legs. Noisy miners are grey with flesh-coloured legs. Both have yellow bills and yellow eye patches. Destroying a noisy miner is a wildlife offence.

What reduces Indian myna numbers:

  • Block access to nest sites in your roof and eaves. Cover gaps, clear dead palm fronds quickly, and bird-proof your gutters. Check for trapped possums before you seal anything permanently.
  • Do not feed them, even by accident. Bring pet food inside, feed livestock where mynas cannot reach the food, and seal compost and food scraps. Bird feeders meant for native birds often end up feeding mynas.
  • Remove nests and eggs, wearing gloves. Indian myna eggs are a distinctive blue-turquoise. No native hollow-nesting bird lays eggs that colour, so if you find them in your roof, you have mynas. Seal the eggs and nest material in a plastic bag and put it in your wheelie bin.
  • Restore native habitat. Mynas prefer cleared, disturbed land. Planting local natives and having less lawn makes your property less attractive to them and more welcoming to native species.

Trapping is also possible. But it needs careful planning, access to humane euthanasia, and enough cooperation with neighbours to make a real difference to local numbers. If you want to set up or join a community action group, the Indian Myna Action Group publishes detailed guidance. For advice on local considerations, call our Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: There are pest animals on Council land or roads near my property. Who do I contact?
items.a:
Contact our Local Laws Team, who coordinate invasive animal control on land and road reserves we manage. Report it using our online service request form or call 1300 697 372.

Useful details to include:

  • the location (GPS or nearest cross street)
  • the species
  • roughly how many animals
  • when you saw them
  • any signs of damage
We do not manage all public land. The Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) manages State-controlled roads, including the New England Highway and Cunningham Highway. Call TMR's Darling Downs office on 07 4639 0777. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service (QPWS) manages national parks (Main Range, Girraween, Sundown). Contact QPWS about pests inside a park.

You can also log sightings in FeralScan. It is free and works as a phone app. The data helps us, the DDMRB and neighbouring landholders coordinate wider control efforts.

tabs.label: Weeds
tabs.intro:
Dealing with weeds on your property? This FAQ covers the plants declared as pests in the Southern Downs, your legal obligations as a landholder, and the practical help Council can offer — including free or low-cost equipment hire.

If you'd rather talk it through, call Council's Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: Do I have to control weeds on my property?
items.a:
Generally, yes, but the duty is more practical than most people expect. Queensland law asks every landholder to take "reasonable and practical" steps to stop invasive plants spreading from their land. You do not have to get rid of every weed.

What is "reasonable and practical" depends on the species, how bad the infestation is, the size of the property, and what the landholder can realistically manage. Treating a small new outbreak of African Boxthorn is reasonable. Hand-pulling every blackberry on 200 hectares of bushland is not.

A few species come with stronger obligations:

  • Blackberry, African Boxthorn and Lantana are restricted invasive plants under the state Biosecurity Act 2014. They must not be sold, given away or released into the environment, and you are expected to actively control them.
  • Firethorn, Green Cestrum and St John's Wort are declared pest plants under our local law. This gives us the power to take further action if needed.

Our Local Laws Team can help you work out what is reasonable for your property. Call 1300 697 372.

items.q: Which weeds are a problem in the Southern Downs?
items.a:
A handful of species cause most of the trouble locally. Each has a Queensland Government fact sheet with photos to help you identify it, life-cycle information and detailed herbicide recommendations.

Restricted invasive plants under the Biosecurity Act 2014 (across Queensland, these cannot be sold, given away or released):

  • African Boxthorn: a spiny shrub that forms thickets too dense to get through, and shelters rabbits and foxes. A Weed of National Significance.
  • Blackberry: forms dense thickets and invades pastures and bushland. Found around Stanthorpe, Warwick and Killarney. A Weed of National Significance.
  • Lantana: common on recently bought or neglected land. It smothers native plants and is toxic to stock.

Declared locally under our Subordinate Local Law No. 7 (we can issue control notices):

  • Firethorn: a spiny garden plant that has escaped into the wild. Common on the Granite Belt between Warwick and the border.
  • Green Cestrum: toxic to cattle, sheep, horses, pigs and poultry. It spreads from its roots and is spread by birds.
  • St John's Wort: makes grazing stock sensitive to sunlight. There are known populations around Stanthorpe.

Other priority species:

  • Tree Pear and other invasive cacti: we lend free Cactus Injectors to landholders to treat these on their own property. See Does Council offer equipment to help me control weeds?

For the full Queensland list of invasive plants, with a fact sheet for each, see Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets. Our own page is Pest Management — Weeds.

items.q: I've found a plant I think might be a weed. How do I identify it?
items.a:
Start with the Queensland Government's free fact sheets: Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets. There is one for every declared and restricted invasive plant, with photos, the features that set it apart, and the plants it is often mistaken for.

If you are still not sure, our Local Laws Team can help. Call 1300 697 372 and describe what you have seen: leaf shape, flower colour, fruit, where it is growing and how tall it is. They may ask for a photo to help identify it.

Be careful using general image-search tools to identify plants. Many invasive plants look like native ones, and getting it wrong either way is a problem: you could destroy a native plant or ignore a declared weed. The Queensland fact sheets are the definitive source.

items.q: What herbicide should I use?
items.a:
Check the Queensland Government fact sheet for your weed: Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets. Each one has a detailed herbicide table with specific products, application rates, situations (pasture, non-crop, native conservation area) and the right season to spray. They are the authoritative source and worth printing before you go to the rural supplies store.

Some general principles:

  • Always read the herbicide label and follow it exactly. Labels are legally binding.
  • Check for permits. Some herbicide uses rely on APVMA (Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority) minor-use permits. Where one applies, the species fact sheet gives the current permit number.
  • Timing matters. Most weeds are best treated while they are actively growing, usually from spring to autumn. Spraying dormant or stressed plants wastes chemical and gives poor results.
  • Move grazing stock out of sprayed areas during and after treatment. Treated plants can become tastier to stock, or more toxic for a while.
  • Some properties are in hazardous chemical areas under the Agricultural Chemicals Distribution Control Act 1966, which restricts certain herbicides. Check before you spray.

Our Local Laws Team can give general advice on how to approach it, but cannot recommend specific commercial products. Call 1300 697 372 to talk it through.

items.q: There are weeds on a Council road near my property. Who do I contact?
items.a:
Contact our Local Laws Team, who coordinate weed control on our roads and land. Report it using our online service request form or call 1300 697 372.

Weeds on the New England Highway or Cunningham Highway? These are State Government roads managed by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR). Contact TMR's Darling Downs office on 07 4639 0777.

items.q: My neighbour has weeds spreading onto my property. Can Council help?
items.a:
Yes. This is a biosecurity matter, not a "neighbour dispute". Every landholder in Queensland has a legal duty to take reasonable steps to stop invasive plants spreading from their land. If your neighbour is not meeting that duty and weeds are spreading onto your property, we can investigate.

First, talk to your neighbour if you feel safe doing so. Often the landholder does not know what is on their property, or does not realise the plant is a problem. A friendly conversation often achieves more than a formal complaint.

If that does not fix it, lodge a service request using our online service request form. Or call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to a Local Laws Officer.

Our Local Laws Team will assess the situation and talk to you about next steps. These may include working with your neighbour directly. For restricted species under the state Biosecurity Act 2014, we may refer the matter to Biosecurity Queensland, part of the Department of Primary Industries (DPI). See the DPI contact page.

items.q: I've been told I have a water leak. How do I find it?
items.a:
You can find many leaks without a plumber. Check inside first. A running toilet is a common cause. Also check all taps, showerheads and washing machine connections.

Outside, look for ground that is unusually green or boggy. This can mean an underground pipe has failed, even when there is no water on the surface. Check garden timers and hose guns too.

The Checking for Water Leaks Fact Sheet explains how to find water leaks yourself, including in underground pipes.

items.q: There's a leak at the meter or on the footpath — is that Council's responsibility?
items.a:
Our side (the meter itself, or the pipe between the water main and the meter): report it to us straight away on 1300 697 372.

Your side (the pipe from the meter into the property): the property owner is responsible for this. You may want to turn off the water at the meter while you arrange a licensed plumber.

Not sure which side it is? Call 1300 697 372 and we can help you work it out.

items.q: Can I get a rates adjustment if I had an unexpected leak?
items.a:
Only in limited cases. Under our Rate Concessions Policy, you can get relief from water consumption charges when:

  • The leak was on our side (the water main, the pipe to the meter, or the meter itself), and we repaired it or confirmed the failure. The rebate covers the extra water above your usual use (at least 10 kilolitres), for one billing period.
  • The leak was a hidden plumbing failure on your side of the meter, on a property connected to the Yangan water network. A licensed plumber must repair it and confirm in a report that the leak could not reasonably have been seen. The rebate is half the extra water, between 10 and 250 kilolitres.

For leaks on your side of the meter anywhere else, there is no relief.

If your property has had a smart water meter for 6 months or more, and the leak could have been picked up through the My SDRC Water portal, we will not grant relief except in exceptional circumstances. Sign up to the portal and set a usage alert. See How can I monitor my water usage between bills?
Act quickly.
  • From when you became aware of the leak, you have 5 business days to investigate and a further 10 business days to repair it.
  • You are taken to be aware 5 business days after we issue a rates notice or high-usage letter, or on the day we call or email you.
  • Apply within 30 days after the due date of the water charge.
  • You can make one claim per property every 5 years. Later claims need records of meter readings taken at least monthly.
  • Applying does not extend the due date or stop interest.

To apply, contact our Revenue Team on 1300 697 372. Have your repair invoice and plumber's report ready.

items.q: Where is my water meter?
items.a: Water meters are usually near the front boundary of the property, close to the street. They are often in a small covered box set into the ground. If you cannot find yours, call 1300 697 372 and we can look up exactly where it is.

items.q: How can I monitor my water usage between bills?
items.a:
Use the My SDRC Water portal. It connects to your Smart Water Meter, so you can see your usage almost as it happens. You can also set your own alert level to catch a leak early.

How to sign up is on page 4 of your rates notice. See also Smart Water Meters.

items.q: I think my water meter is wrong. Can it be tested?
items.a:
Yes. Call 1300 697 372. Our field staff can check the meter on site. With no water being used, they run 100 litres through a test meter and compare the readings. If your meter is within 5%, it is taken to be accurate.

Before you call, try the hidden leak test in I've been told I have a water leak. How do I find it? or the Checking for Water Leaks Fact Sheet. A meter that keeps moving while nothing is running usually means a leak, not a faulty meter.

If you are still not satisfied, you can ask for a formal test. We fit a replacement meter, with at least 48 hours' written notice before the water is turned off, and send yours to an accredited laboratory.

  • 20mm and 25mm meters: $722
  • larger meters: quoted

We refund the fee if the meter is faulty. We then work out the charge for the affected period from your average daily use in earlier billing periods.

items.q: Is there help with water costs for home dialysis?
items.a:
Yes. If someone at the property has regular haemodialysis treatment at home, our Home Haemodialysis Water Allowance can help. Each reading period, we credit the property's rates account with the cost of 65 kL of water, at the first level water rate.

Fill in the Annual Application for Home Haemodialysis Water Allowance on our Rate & Property Forms page, and attach:

  • a letter to us from the patient's doctor, renal specialist or Queensland Health haemodialysis centre manager, confirming the patient has treatment at home, how many hours it takes and how often
  • proof that the patient lives permanently at the property and pays the water consumption charges
The allowance ends on 30 June each year, so apply again at the start of each financial year. Tell us in writing if treatment stops or the patient moves.

The credit goes to the property's rates account. If the patient is not the owner, the patient cannot claim it back from us directly.

With the patient's permission, we keep their contact details so we can warn them about planned water interruptions and treat faults as a priority. Make sure the patient's dialysis provider has trained them in managing an interruption to supply.

items.q: Can I connect my property to Council's water and sewer?
items.a:
It depends on whether your property is inside our water or sewer service area. There are 2 quick ways to check:

  1. Check the map. Open the Online Mapping tool and search for your address. Switch on the Underground Infrastructure module and turn on the Water/Sewer Catchment Overlay.
  2. Check your rates notice. Look at the breakdown of charges on page 2. If your property is already in the service area and paying to have the service available, it will show a water access charge or an unconnected sewerage charge.

If you are inside the service area, you can apply for a connection. See How do I apply for a water connection, and what does it cost? and How do I apply for a sewer connection, and what does it cost?

If you are outside it, we must first approve extending the service area, and you pay the cost of extending the main to your property. Email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au or call 1300 697 372 for advice about your property.

If you cannot connect to sewer, you will need an on-site sewerage facility. See What about sewerage? Do I need a septic tank or a treatment plant? on the Building Rural tab.

A standard connection is one 20mm metered water service per lot, from one of our water mains of at least 100mm. We assess these separately: larger services, extra connections, connections to smaller mains, and anything that needs a main extended. Call 1300 697 372 before you apply.

If you have been paying the water access charge and your application to connect is refused, our Water Infrastructure Policy entitles you to a refund of the access charges you paid while you owned the property.

items.q: How do I find out how deep the sewer is, or exactly where it runs?

The Underground Infrastructure module in our Online Mapping tool is a good first look, but it will not confirm how deep a pipe is.

To have us find a pipe on site and confirm its depth, fill in an Application for Private Works on our Roads & Works Forms page. We inspect the site and then quote the cost.

items.q: Can I disconnect from town water or sewer?
items.a:

To disconnect a vacant lot, apply on our Water & Sewerage Forms page.

items.q: Where do I take this? — Recycle Mate does the thinking for you
items.a:
Recycle Mate is a free app and web tool that tells you exactly how and where to get rid of almost anything. Take a photo or type in the item, and it shows you places in the Southern Downs that take it. These include our waste facilities, supermarkets that collect soft plastics or batteries, pharmacies that take unused medicines, and charity shops that accept reusable items.

It is the fastest way to answer "where does this go?" without calling us. Download it from your app store, or use our SDRC Recycle Mate page.

If Recycle Mate does not cover your item, or you want to double-check, call us on 1300 697 372 and our waste team can advise.

items.q: What day is my bin collected?
items.a:
Search for your address in our SDRC online mapping tool to find your bin day, or call 1300 697 372. Your collection day depends on your property address.

Collection days may change on public holidays. We publish any changes in advance.

items.q: What goes in which bin?
items.a:
Red or green lid (general waste, weekly): kitchen and food waste, general household rubbish, plastic bags and cling wrap, nappies, and polystyrene foam.

Yellow lid (recycling, fortnightly): paper and cardboard, steel and aluminium cans, hard plastic bottles and containers (lids off), and glass bottles and jars (lids off).

Not sure about an item? Use Recycle Mate, which is made for exactly this. See Where do I take this? — Recycle Mate does the thinking for you.

Never put batteries in either bin. They can cause serious truck fires. See How do I dispose of batteries, phones, and e-waste?

Full details are on our Residential Waste & Recycling — SDRC page.

items.q: My bin wasn't collected. What do I do?
items.a:
Lodge a request using our online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Cleanaway will come back for it before your next regular collection day.

Before you lodge a request, check that the bin was on the kerb by 6:00am and was not blocked by a parked car. These are the most common reasons a bin is missed.

items.q: My bin is damaged or missing. Can I get a replacement?
items.a:
Yes. Lodge a request using our online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Give your address and describe the problem.

We repair damaged bins where we can. If a bin cannot be fixed, or has been stolen, we replace it.

items.q: I'm elderly or have a disability and can't put my bins out. Is there help available?
items.a:
Yes. Our Infirm Collection Service is for residents who cannot put their bins out because of age, disability or a medical condition that limits their movement. Cleanaway drivers collect the bins from the property and put them back once emptied, as part of their normal round.

The service is only available if nobody else at the property can put the bins out.

To apply, email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au with the subject line ATTN Waste Team. Attach:

  • a letter asking for the service
  • a letter or medical certificate from a registered health practitioner confirming your situation

items.q: I don't have a bin service — can I get one?

It depends where your property is in the Designated Waste Collection Area. There are 3 categories:

  • Compulsory: you must have the service, and the charge is on your rates notice.
  • Opt-In / Opt-Out: you can choose whether to have the service.
  • Voluntary: you can ask for a service, and Cleanaway decides whether it can service the property, based on its route and access.

To ask for a new service, lodge a New waste bin for single unit dwelling request in our online request system. The charges are added to your rates notice. If your request is approved, we deliver the bins to the property.

If your property is outside the collection area, you can take your waste to one of our waste facilities, or use a rural bin compound if there is one for your area. These are locked bin compounds with no staff on site. You open them with a key, which we only give to approved residents in the catchment area. items.q: How do I dispose of green waste, garden clippings, and trickle tape?
items.a:
Green waste, such as grass clippings, prunings and small branches, can go in your red or green lid general waste bin. Do not put green waste in the yellow recycling bin.

You can take larger loads to one of our waste facilities. Green waste is free for residents, but there is a fee for commercial green waste. Composting or mulching at home is also a great option. See our Worm Farming and Composting fact sheets.

Trickle tape (T-tape): you can bring clean trickle tape to the Stanthorpe Waste Management Facility for recycling, free of charge. The tape must be separated from plastic mulch, with as little soil, roots and other organic matter on it as possible. Contaminated tape cannot be recycled, and commercial operators pay landfill fees for it. The site supervisors will show you where to put it when you arrive.

Do not dump green waste in bushland, on verges or in waterways. It spreads pest plants, fuels bushfires and can draw wildlife onto roadsides. See Someone has dumped rubbish on my land or in a public place. How do I report it?

items.q: How do I dispose of batteries, phones, and e-waste?
items.a:
Never put batteries in a kerbside bin. They can short-circuit, catch fire, and damage trucks or facilities. Batteries are one of the fastest-growing causes of waste fires in Australia.

Batteries under 5kg: we have partnered with Ecobatt, and there are battery collection containers at all our waste facilities that have staff on site. Tape over the terminals, especially on lithium batteries, and hand the battery to an attendant rather than dropping it in. Accepted types include:

  • household alkaline: AA, AAA, C, D, PP3 and button cells
  • lithium and rechargeable: mobile phones, laptops, tablets, cameras, e-cigarettes and vapes, portable tools, e-scooters and e-bikes, and power banks
  • lead acid: car, vehicle and caravan batteries. Make sure the caps are tight, and speak to an attendant if the casing is damaged

If a battery is damaged, speak to a facility attendant before you bring it in.

E-waste (computers, TVs and accessories) is accepted for recycling at all our waste facilities that have staff on site.

Recycle Mate also lists private drop-off points. Many pharmacies, supermarkets and electronics shops run their own battery and phone collections, which may be closer than a waste facility.

To find the nearest drop-off point, use Recycle Mate, or see our Waste Facilities page for locations and opening hours.

items.q: Where do I take items I can't put in the bin — mattresses, whitegoods, chemicals, asbestos?
items.a:
Start with Recycle Mate. It will often find an option that is closer or cheaper than our facilities. Our waste facilities take most other items. Locations, opening hours and what each site accepts are on the Waste Facilities page.

Free at our facilities: scrap metal, clean concrete and bricks, e-waste, empty agvet chemical containers (drumMUSTER), used motor oil at some sites, and clean timber pallets.

You pay a fee for: general household waste, mattresses, tyres, whitegoods, and construction and demolition waste. The fees are in our annual Fees & Charges schedule.

Asbestos: you must book ahead. Asbestos must be double-bagged in 200-micron plastic, clearly labelled, and booked with us before you bring it in. Facility staff cannot accept asbestos without a booking. Call 1300 697 372 to book.

Pets that have died: small pets (birds, fish, guinea pigs) can go in the general waste bin. Take larger pets to the closest waste facility that accepts them. Burial is only available at the Warwick Waste Management Facility. You must tell us in advance about bulk loads.

Ammunition, explosives and old fireworks must never go in any bin or waste facility. Contact the Queensland Explosives Inspectorate on 1300 739 868 (24-hour hotline).

items.q: Someone has dumped rubbish on my land or in a public place. How do I report it?
items.a:
Lodge a service request using our online service request form or call 1300 697 372. On the form, you can pin the exact location on the map and attach photos.

Illegal dumping is leaving 200 litres or more of waste (about a wheelie bin's worth) where it should not be. This includes bushland, roadsides, waterways, outside charity bins, on the kerb outside collection times, or in the wrong place at a waste facility.

Give us as much detail as you can:

  • the time, date and place, and a description of the waste
  • the vehicle's registration, make, model, colour or anything that stands out
  • a description of the person (where they were in the vehicle, clothing, gender)
Do not approach the person dumping the waste. Only take photos if it is safe.

Fines are significant. Individuals and companies can face large on-the-spot fines, and much higher penalties if the matter goes to court. The current amounts are in the Illegal Dumping fact sheet.

Worth knowing: you can get rid of almost all household waste at our facilities for free. Doing it properly costs much less than the fine for dumping.

items.q: I've spotted what looks like trade waste pollution — chemicals in a waterway, oil drums leaking, or unauthorised dumping of business waste. How do I report it?
items.a:
Lodge a service request using our online service request form. You do not need an account, and you can attach photos and pin the location on a map. Or call 1300 697 372.

If it is happening now and may be an immediate risk to people, animals or waterways, call 000 for police or fire, then tell us afterwards.

Trade waste and environmental pollution are more serious than ordinary illegal dumping, and we take them seriously. Examples include:

  • dumped solvents or chemicals
  • oil drums or tanks leaking onto land or into waterways
  • contaminated runoff from a workshop or industrial site
  • sediment escaping from a building site
  • unauthorised landfilling on private land

Useful details to include:

  • the time, date and exact location (a dropped pin or street address)
  • what you saw: the substance, type of container, smell, colour and amount
  • vehicle details, if relevant: make, model, colour and registration
  • photos, if you can take them safely

Our regulatory services team investigates illegal dumping of trade waste. Where state environmental laws apply, we work with Queensland Government authorities. Larger or hazardous incidents are usually investigated jointly. Reporting these matters protects waterways, soil and your community, so do not assume someone else has reported it.

Do not approach the source. Only take photos if it is safe. Some dumped substances are genuinely dangerous. Your safety and an accurate report matter more than confronting whoever is responsible.

items.q: There's an abandoned shopping trolley near my property. Whose problem is it?
items.a:
Almost always the retailer's, not ours. Most major supermarkets and hardware chains in the Southern Downs (Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, IGA, Bunnings) use trolley collection services that pick up reported trolleys the same day or the next day.

What to do:

  • Look for a sticker on the trolley with a phone number or QR code. This is the fastest way. The trolley collection contractor will arrange to pick it up.
  • If there is no sticker, or you cannot tell which retailer it belongs to, call the nearest store of that chain. They will arrange collection.
  • If a trolley is left for a long time, or trolleys keep being dumped in the same place, lodge a service request with us. We can follow up with the retailer under local nuisance provisions, but this is slower than going to the retailer directly.

Report trolleys in waterways or storm drains, or causing an immediate hazard (blocking footpaths, on roads), to us on 1300 697 372 and we will act quickly.

tabs.label: Roads

items.q: How to check whether a road is managed by Council or Transport and Main Roads?
items.a:
Search for the closest street address in the Road Lookup - QLDTraffic tool. It shows whether we or the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) look after the road.

As a general rule, TMR looks after highways and major roads, and we look after most urban streets and rural roads.

items.q: Are damaged roads Council's or the State Government's responsibility?
items.a:
Not all roads in the region are ours to look after. The Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) manages the major highways.

  • State roads (New England Highway, Cunningham Highway and other TMR roads): report urgent issues to TMR on 13 19 40
  • Rail crossings and railway tracks: report level crossing faults or safety incidents to Queensland Rail on 1800 079 303. For other railway enquiries, call 13 16 17
  • Our roads: lodge a request with us, as in How do I report a pothole or road damage on a council managed road?

Not sure? Call us on 1300 697 372 and we can help.

items.q: How do I report a pothole or road damage on a council managed road?
items.a:
Report it online using our online service request form. The form has a map where you can mark exactly where the pothole is. You can also call us on 1300 697 372.

Tell us the street name, the nearest landmark and roughly how big the pothole or damage is.

items.q: How do I check if a road is closed?
items.a:
Check the SDRC Disaster Dashboard. It has current road closures and a map with flood camera images of the main crossings. It is the most up-to-date source during weather events.

For State roads, check Queensland Traffic.

items.q: My vehicle was damaged by a road defect. Can I make a claim?
items.a:
Yes. Send us a letter of demand that includes:

  • your name
  • the time and place of the incident
  • what was damaged
  • any supporting evidence, such as photos or quotes

Address road-related claims to ATTN: Governance, Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370, or email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

tabs.label: Disputes

items.q: What disputes can Council help with?
items.a:
Our Local Laws team can investigate:

  • noise that keeps happening, such as barking dogs, loud machinery or amplified music
  • dust, smoke, odour or light pollution
  • water pollution from a neighbouring property
  • building work without approval, or illegal use of a structure
  • unlawful land use

Make a complaint using our online service request form or call us on 1300 697 372.

items.q: What disputes are outside Council's jurisdiction?
items.a:
Some common disputes are private matters that we cannot mediate or enforce. These include:

  • boundary and fencing disputes
  • trees crossing property lines
  • parking complaints outside the regulated Warwick CBD parking area (these are a police matter)
  • easement disputes

The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) is often the right place to take these. Visit qcat.qld.gov.au or call 1300 753 228.

items.q: My neighbour's tree drops branches, blocks light, or damages my fence. What can I do?
items.a:
Tree disputes between neighbours are a private matter that we cannot mediate. They are covered by the Queensland Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011.

What to do:

  1. Talk to your neighbour first. Most tree problems are sorted out once the owner knows about them.
  2. If you cannot agree, you can serve a formal notice on the tree owner under the Act, asking them to act.
  3. If that does not work, you can take the matter to QCAT. Visit qcat.qld.gov.au or call 1300 753 228.

You can trim branches that hang over your property, up to the boundary line. You pay for this yourself, and you must not harm the tree's health. Give the trimmings back to the tree owner. Do not dump them.

Trees on our land or on road reserves are different. Lodge a service request and one of our officers will assess the tree. Never trim or remove one of our trees yourself.

items.q: I have a boundary or fencing dispute with my neighbour. What now?
items.a:
Fences between two residential properties are covered by the Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011, not by us. As a general rule, both neighbours share the cost of a "sufficient dividing fence" equally. What counts as sufficient depends on the zone and the existing fence.

What to do:

  1. Talk to your neighbour first. Agree on what needs doing and get a quote from a fencing contractor.
  2. If you cannot agree, serve a formal Notice to Fence on your neighbour. The Queensland Government has templates.
  3. If you still have not agreed 30 days after the notice, either of you can apply to QCAT for a decision. Visit qcat.qld.gov.au or call 1300 753 228.

A boundary dispute (where the fence should go) is separate from a fencing dispute (who pays for what). If you are not sure where the boundary is, a licensed surveyor can confirm it. Our online mapping shows cadastral boundaries for reference, but it does not replace a survey.

items.q: My neighbour's shed or extension looks unapproved. How do I report it?
items.a:
Unlike most neighbour disputes, we can investigate building work done without approval. If you think a structure was built without the building or planning approval it needed, make a complaint using our online service request form or call us on 1300 697 372.

Give us as much detail as you can:

  • the address
  • a description of the structure
  • when it was built, if you know
  • why you think it is unapproved

Our Building Compliance team will investigate. If the work is unapproved, they may issue a notice requiring it to be certified after the fact, or removed. This takes time. You should not expect a same-day outcome.

Not every structure needs approval. Small sheds (under 10m²), fences under 2m and retaining walls under 1m may be self-assessable. The Building Rural and Building Urban tabs have the details.

items.q: Someone is running a business from a residential property. Can Council investigate?
items.a:
Yes. We can investigate "unlawful land use" under the Planning Scheme.

Some home-based businesses are allowed. These are usually small, low-impact businesses that do not bring more traffic, noise or signage than a normal home. Others need planning approval, or are not allowed in residential zones at all.

Signs that a business has gone too far include:

  • commercial vehicle traffic
  • employees coming and going
  • customer parking
  • commercial signs
  • industrial noise
  • activities that change the character of the property

Make a complaint using our online service request form or call us on 1300 697 372. Our Planning Compliance team will investigate.

tabs.label: Rates & Payments

items.q: My rate notice shows a new “NPPR” category. What is it?
items.a:
NPPR stands for Non-Principal Place of Residence. It is our new general rate category for residential properties that are not the owner's main home, such as rentals, holiday houses and second homes. We introduced it in the 2026–27 budget.

The NPPR Rates tab explains how the rate is calculated, how we decide whether your property is NPPR, and how to object if you think your property is in the wrong category.

items.q: How do I pay my rates?
items.a:
You can pay your rates:

  • online through SDRC Online Payments
  • by BPAY, using the biller code and reference on your notice
  • in person at our Warwick or Stanthorpe office
  • by post, with a cheque payable to Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370

items.q: I'm struggling to pay my rates. What can I do?
items.a:
Call us as early as you can on 1300 697 372. The sooner you contact us, the more options there are.

Options may include paying by instalments, hardship provisions or, in exceptional circumstances, deferring payment. Our Payment Difficulties page has more information.

items.q: How do I receive my rates notice by email instead of post?
items.a:
Scan the QR code on page 2 of your rates notice to register for eNotices. Your future notices will come by email. It is faster, paperless, and we let you know as soon as your notice is ready.

You can also sign up online. See our How to Receive your Rate Notices via Email page.

items.q: How do I check my rates balance?
items.a:
There are 2 ways:

  • Call us on 1300 697 372 and give your property address or rates account number. Customer Service can tell you your current balance over the phone.
  • Sign up for eProperty, a free online portal where you can see your current balance, payment history and rates notices at any time. Set up an account on our eProperty registration page. You will need a recent rates notice to confirm your details.

items.q: When do my rates notices arrive in the post?
items.a:
We send out 2 rates notices a year:

  • First notice: arrives in February or March and covers the first half of the financial year.
  • Second notice: arrives in August or September and covers the second half.

If your notice is more than 3 weeks late, call us on 1300 697 372. We can check your postal address and send you a replacement copy.

To avoid postal delays, you can get your notices by email instead. See How do I receive my rates notice by email instead of post?

items.q: I've received a supplementary rates notice. What does it mean?
items.a:
A supplementary rates notice is an extra charge we issue between the regular 6-monthly notices. It usually means something has changed in how your property is rated. The most common reason is the sale or subdivision of bulk-assessed land.

What is bulk assessment? In rural zones, several neighbouring lots with the same owner are often rated together as a single Property ID (PID). The State Government values them together, usually at a lower rate per hectare than if they were valued one by one. When one of those lots is sold or subdivided, it gets its own PID and is valued on its own. The new valuation is usually higher than its previous share, so the rates change.

Why is the bill higher than I expected?

  • A standard rates notice covers 6 months. A supplementary notice may cover a longer period, sometimes a full year or more, depending on when the change took effect. Check the dates on the notice before you compare it with a regular one.
  • If the land was subdivided or split from bulk-assessed land, the higher valuation comes from the State Government valuing each lot separately. We cannot reduce a valuation set by the State.

What can I do if I disagree with the valuation? The Queensland Department of Resources sets property valuations, not us. You have 60 days from the date of the valuation notice to lodge a formal objection with the Department. We cannot step in, but Customer Service can help you understand your supplementary notice. Call 1300 697 372 if you want to talk through the charge.

Property sale settlements: In a typical settlement, the solicitors adjust the sale price so the seller and buyer each pay the rates for the part of the period they own the property. Neither of you usually needs to contact us. The Titles Office updates the owner's name on the property automatically. When bulk-assessed land is split or sold, though, the seller usually pays all rates in full before settlement. This is because the property usually cannot be revalued fast enough to issue a supplementary notice during settlement.

items.q: What do the different charges on my rates notice mean?
items.a:
Our Rates & Charges Explained page explains each line on your notice: what it pays for and how it is worked out. For a question about your own notice, call us on 1300 697 372 and a rates officer can go through it with you.

For water and sewerage charges, including what changes when you connect, see How much will connecting to town water and sewer add to my rates? on the Water tab.

items.q: Can I give authority to someone to deal with Council about my rates for me?
items.a:
Yes. Anyone can pay the rates on a property. You do not need to be the owner. But we can only give out information about the property, or refund money, to the owner or to someone the owner has authorised.

There are 3 ways someone else can act for an owner:

  • Agent. The owner signs our Authority to Appoint an Agent form. It names the person who can deal with us for them about that property.
  • Power of attorney. If the owner can no longer manage their affairs, a person appointed under a power of attorney (including an enduring power of attorney) can deal with us and get information about the property. Give us a certified copy of the signed power of attorney documents. A power of attorney ends when the owner dies.
  • Deceased estate. The executor gives us a certified copy of the will and a certified copy of the death certificate.

Send the form or documents to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au, or call 1300 697 372 and ask for the revenue team.
