tabs.label: NPPR Rates
tabs.intro:
From the 2026/27 budget, Council has a new general rate category: Non-Principal Place of Residence (NPPR). It applies to residential properties that are not the owner's main home — for example rentals, holiday houses and second homes. Each person can have only one principal place of residence (PPR); any other residential property they own is rated as NPPR. Council introduced the category to avoid a larger general rate rise for owner-occupiers, whose increase was held below CPI.

If the property is your main home and your notice says NPPR, you can object — the test and the process are below.

stepper.label: STEP 1
stepper.text: Check the category on your rate notice

stepper.label: STEP 2
stepper.text: Run the three-part PPR test

stepper.label: STEP 3
stepper.text: Gather your evidence

stepper.label: STEP 4
stepper.text: Lodge your objection within 31 days

stepper.label: STEP 5
stepper.text: CEO decision within 60 days (pay your notice meanwhile)

items.q: What is the NPPR category, and why was it introduced?
items.a:
NPPR stands for Non-Principal Place of Residence. It is a general rate category for residential properties that are not the owner's main home. We introduced it in the 2026–27 budget. A person can have only one principal place of residence. All their other residential properties fall into NPPR.

We made the change to keep general rates lower for owner-occupiers, instead of spreading a larger increase across everyone. The 2026–27 budget kept the median increase for owner-occupiers below CPI, lower than many Queensland councils. As a result, residential and business rates stayed lower. Before adopting the budget, we ran extensive community engagement, which set out the proposed NPPR category.

The NPPR category affects only the general rate part of your notice. Charges for water access and usage, sewerage, waste collection and the emergency services levy are worked out separately. Our Revenue Statement has the current amounts for those.

To check whether your property is NPPR, see Is my property a principal place of residence or NPPR? The three-part test. For anything else, contact our revenue team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: How is the NPPR general rate calculated, and how much more is it?
items.a:
The NPPR rate is 20% higher in the dollar than the matching owner-occupier rate. Like all general rates, it is worked out from your land valuation. There are 2 NPPR sub-categories, split at a land value of $239,000:

CategoryLand valueNPPR rate (per $1 of land value)Owner-occupier rate
NPPR 1Less than $239,0001.103c0.919c
NPPR 2Greater than $239,0000.882c0.735c

NPPR 1 properties also have a minimum general rate charge of $1,700.00 a year.

Two other things affect the final figure:

  • Your land value may have changed since your last notice. If so, the Valuer-General should have told you. You can also check your current land valuation online.
  • There is currently a 35% cap on how much your rates charge can rise from one year to the next.

items.q: Is my property a principal place of residence or NPPR? The three-part test
items.a:
Your property is your principal place of residence (PPR) if all 3 of these are true:

  • 1. A natural person owns it (or holds a life tenancy). Not a company, trust, person as trustee, incorporated association, personal representative or deceased estate.
  • 2. You live there for at least 245 days a year (about 8 months), and intend to keep doing so.
  • 3. It is a lawful dwelling (Class 1a). This is shown by a Form 21 Final Inspection Certificate, or a current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation under our Subordinate Local Law 1.3. The objection form calls this a Temporary Home Permit.

If any one of the 3 is not true, the property is NPPR. Remember, each person can have only one PPR. Every other residential property you own is NPPR, even if family members live there.

Life tenant — a person who holds a legal right to use, occupy or benefit from a property for the rest of their life (for example, under a will).

If you think your property is in the wrong category, see I believe my property has been wrongly categorised. How do I object? To talk it through, contact our revenue team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: How do common situations get categorised? (trusts, aged care, Airbnb, vacant land, deceased estates)
items.a:
Some common situations:

  • A company or trust owns it, and I live there: a property 100% owned by a company or trust is NPPR. The ownership test requires a natural person, with no exceptions. This includes where someone living there holds a life tenancy.
  • The owner is in aged care: the home stays PPR if the owner lived there before going into care, intends to return, and the home stays empty (not rented out).
  • Short-term accommodation (for example, Airbnb): licensed short-term accommodation is rated in a Commercial category, not NPPR. A licence is required. If the owner also lives on site, it may still count as PPR. Contact our revenue team on 1300 697 372 to discuss it.
  • Vacant land, or a home being built: NPPR until a Form 21 is issued and you are living there. The exception is a current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation, which makes it PPR. See the Building Rural tab for living on site during a build.
  • Mail goes to a PO box: that alone does not make a property NPPR. Use the 3-part test, and object if the category is wrong.
  • Deceased estate: NPPR, unless a life tenant under the will lives in the property. That can make it PPR.

To check your own property, see Is my property a principal place of residence or NPPR? The three-part test.

items.q: I believe my property has been wrongly categorised. How do I object?
items.a:
You can lodge a Notice of Objection Against Categorisation under the Local Government Regulation 2012. The only ground for objecting is that the category is factually wrong. For example, the property really is your main home, or it belongs in a different category for some other reason. Disagreeing with the policy itself is not a ground for objection. To give feedback on the policy, see I disagree with the NPPR policy itself. How do I have my say?

There are 2 ways to lodge:

  • Online: lodge an online service request and choose “Notice of Objection Against Categorisation”. Have your rate notice with you. You will need your Property ID, address, current rating category and land use code, which are all on the notice.
  • Paper form: download the Notice of Objection Against Categorisation form. Email the completed form and your evidence to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au, or post it to The CEO, Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370.

Timing: you must lodge your objection within 31 days of the issue date on your rate notice, or longer if we allow it. Rate notices are issued every 6 months, so find the issue date on your latest notice and count 31 days from there.

Your objection must say which category you think the land belongs in, and set out the facts that support your claim. For what to include, see What evidence do I need to include with my objection?

items.q: What evidence do I need to include with my objection?
items.a:
You must include evidence. We treat an objection without it as incomplete and decline it.

Proof you live at the property (needed to change to a residential or PPR category), either:

  • confirmation that you are enrolled to vote at the address (check at check.aec.gov.au) plus one other legal document, or
  • 2 or more current legal documents showing the address, such as an electricity or phone bill, vehicle registration renewal, insurance policy or bank statement

Proof the dwelling is lawful (where this applies):

  • for dwellings built after 1 January 2000: a Form 21 Final Inspection Certificate or equivalent
  • for dwellings built before 2000: proof of the dwelling's age (a building approval, aerial imagery, Form 21 or equivalent), or a search of our building records, or both
  • for temporary homes: a copy of your current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation
If your property is currently recorded under a vacant land use code (01A or 06A), you must also include the Form 21 to show a lawful dwelling exists.

To lodge, see I believe my property has been wrongly categorised. How do I object?

items.q: What happens after I lodge my objection?
items.a:
Our Chief Executive Officer reviews your objection within 60 days of receiving it, and makes one of 3 decisions:

  • put the property in the land use and rating category you asked for
  • put it in a different land use or rating category, or both
  • deny the objection

We tell you the outcome in writing. If you are not happy with the decision, you can appeal by filing a Notice of Appeal at the Land Court registry, in the form approved by the Land Court. You must do this within 42 days of receiving the decision notice.

To ask about an objection you have lodged, contact our revenue team on 1300 697 372.

items.q: Do I still have to pay my rates while the objection is being decided?
items.a:
Yes. Under section 88(e) of the Local Government Regulation 2012, you must still pay the amount on your rate notice while we consider an objection. Objecting does not pause payment.

Pay in full by the due date, or you lose the 7.5% discount for paying on time. The discount does not apply to payments received after the due date, whatever the outcome of your objection.

If your objection succeeds, we adjust your rates and deal with any overpayment on your account.

If paying in full is difficult, see I can't afford the increase. What are my options?

items.q: I can't afford the increase. What are my options?
items.a:
The main option is a Payment Agreement. It gives you rates relief by putting off all interest charges and legal recovery action from the date you apply until 30 June of the current financial year. You can choose to pay weekly, fortnightly, monthly, or as a lump sum before 30 June.

We set up payment agreements once your rates notice has been issued. So when your notice arrives, call us on 1300 697 372 to arrange one.

See the Payment Agreements & Rates Relief page for details, including hardship provisions. There is more general guidance on the Rates & Payments tab.

items.q: My land is used for primary production (farming). Is the objection form the right process?
items.a:
No. You cannot use the objection form to move a property between a Primary Production rating category and any other category.

Instead, send an Application for Concessional Valuation to the Department of Natural Resources and Mines, Manufacturing and Regional and Rural Development. If the land is no longer used for primary production, notify the Department instead. The application is at www.nrmmrrd.qld.gov.au.

If your property is given a new valuation, we update our records and your rating category to match.

items.q: I disagree with the NPPR policy itself. How do I have my say?
items.a:
Give feedback through our formal feedback and complaints process. You can lodge an online service request or call us on 1300 697 372. You can comment on the NPPR category as a policy decision, or on the objection process itself.

An objection only deals with whether your property's category is factually correct. It is not the way to give feedback on the policy.

We welcome community discussion on the change and will keep answering questions raised at community meetings. In the meantime, it is still worth checking your property is in the right category. The 3-part test in Is my property a principal place of residence or NPPR? The three-part test takes a minute, and our staff can help you lodge an objection if your property is in the wrong category.

tabs.label: Visiting & Camping
tabs.intro:
Visiting the Southern Downs? This tab covers the practical questions — where you can camp, what permits you need, where to empty a caravan tank — and points to the pages that go into detail.

Council runs the dam reserves, the two campgrounds and the dump points. Fishing and fossicking permits are Queensland Government schemes, and events, private caravan parks and general visitor information come from Southern Downs & Granite Belt Tourism.

items.q: What dams can I visit in the Southern Downs?
items.a:
We manage recreation areas at 3 dams. Each allows different activities.

  • Leslie Dam (Washpool Road, west of Warwick): camping at Washpool Camping Reserve, plus swimming, boating, water skiing, sailing, canoeing and fishing.
  • Connolly Dam (Silverwood, south of Warwick): camping, swimming and canoeing. Only boats without motors are allowed, but electric motors are fine.
  • Storm King Dam (near Stanthorpe): day use, boating and fishing. There is no camping at Storm King Dam.
Storm King Dam is sometimes closed to the public when the water is hired for a water sport competition. Spectators are still welcome on the foreshore.

For camping at the dams, see Where can I camp in the region? or our Caravan & Camping Information page.

items.q: Do I need a permit to fish in the dams?
items.a:
Yes, if you are fishing a stocked impoundment. Leslie, Storm King and Connolly dams are stocked. Everyone aged 18 or over needs a Stocked Impoundment Permit Scheme (SIPS) permit before fishing them.

SIPS is a Queensland Government scheme, not one of ours. You can buy a permit online. The money goes towards maintaining and improving recreational fishing in stocked impoundments, and towards running the scheme.

Before you travel, check the Queensland Government's list of stocked impoundment locations. That list is the authority on which waters need a permit, and it is updated from time to time.

items.q: Can I take a boat out on the dams?
items.a:
Leslie Dam and Storm King Dam: yes. You no longer need a separate boating permit from us.

Connolly Dam: only boats without motors, such as canoes and kayaks. Electric motors are allowed. Petrol and other powered boats are not.

You need a permit to fish. See Do I need a permit to fish in the dams?

items.q: Where can I go fossicking?
items.a:
You need a fossicking licence from the Queensland Government before you fossick. You can buy one online.

A licence does not tell you where you can dig. The State decides which areas are open for fossicking. To fossick on private land, you also need the landholder's permission. Check that the area you are going to is open before you travel.

items.q: Where can I camp in the region?
items.a:
We run 2 campgrounds, both at dams:

  • Washpool Camping Reserve at Leslie Dam: 80 sites, powered and unpowered. You must book.
  • Connolly Dam Camping Ground: 20 unpowered sites, first come, first served.

You can also stay overnight for short periods in 3 of our parks. See Can I stay overnight in a Council park?

For private and commercial campgrounds, see the Southern Downs & Granite Belt caravan, camping and holiday parks listing.

items.q: What's at Washpool Camping Reserve (Leslie Dam)?
items.a:
Washpool Camping Reserve is at the southern end of Leslie Dam, on Washpool Road, Warwick 4370.

Sites: 34 powered and 46 unpowered, including drive-through sites for caravans of any size. You can stay for up to 7 nights. Check in after 12:00pm and check out before 11:00am.

Facilities: 2 toilet blocks with accessible facilities, hot and cold showers, a caravan dump point, clean drinking water and ice. You can swim, canoe, water ski, sail and fish (you need a permit to fish).

Booking: you must book. Call the caretaker on 0427 026 216 between 12pm and 5pm, seven days a week. You cannot book online.

Full details are on the Washpool Reserve Camping Area page.

items.q: What's at Connolly Dam Camping Ground?
items.a:
Connolly Dam Camping Ground is at 1010 Connolly Dam Road, Silverwood, Warwick 4370. Part of Connolly Dam Road is gravel, and all the access roads inside the grounds are gravel.

Sites: 20 unpowered grass sites, suitable for self-contained caravans and tents. Sites are not marked out. They are first come, first served, for stays of up to 7 days.

Facilities: 1 toilet block with accessible facilities, hot showers on a timer and a caravan dump point. You can swim, and canoe without a motor.

Booking: you cannot book ahead. You register yourself on site: look for the registration box with camping forms. Our officers visit every day to collect payment and check that campers have registered correctly.

Full details are on the Connolly Dam Camping Ground page.

items.q: What does camping cost?
items.a:
Connolly Dam and Washpool Reserve charge the same camping site fee, per camper per night.

Camping FeesFee
Adult (18 and over), per night$15.80
Child (4 to 17 years), per night$8.50

The overflow area at Washpool, for self-contained caravans and recreational vehicles, costs less.

We set fees each year, and they change on 1 July. The Fees & Charges schedule always has the current fees.

items.q: Can I bring my dog?
items.a:
No. Dogs, cats and other pets are not allowed at Washpool Camping Reserve or Connolly Dam Camping Ground. Horses and livestock are not allowed either.

If you are travelling with a pet, try the private caravan and holiday parks listed by Southern Downs & Granite Belt Tourism. Each park sets its own rules, so check with the park directly.

items.q: Can I have a campfire?
items.a:
Washpool Camping Reserve: yes, in the drums provided, and for cooking only. Firewood is not supplied, so bring your own. Bonfires and fires left unattended are not allowed.

Connolly Dam Camping Ground: no. Campfires and bonfires are not allowed at any time.

Fire restrictions apply and can change at short notice. Check the current restrictions before you light anything, even in a drum provided.

The Washpool campfire rules are on our Washpool Reserve Camping Area page.

items.q: What are the campground rules?
items.a:
These rules apply at both our campgrounds:

  • All plants and animals are protected.
  • Vehicles must stay on formed roads and other marked areas.
  • There is a noise curfew from 10:30pm to 6:00am.
  • You can only camp in marked areas.

Not allowed at either campground: pets, horses and livestock, glass bottles, explosives and weapons, and unregistered motor vehicles.

Also at Washpool: no bonfires or fires left unattended, no camping or generators beyond the tree line, and no trespassing on neighbouring properties.

Also at Connolly Dam: no campfires at all, no camping beyond the high water mark, and no powered boats except electric ones.

Full details are on the Washpool Reserve Camping Area and Connolly Dam Camping Ground pages. For Washpool bookings and questions, call the caretaker on 0427 026 216 between 12pm and 5pm, seven days a week.

items.q: Can I camp at Storm King Dam?
items.a:
No. There are no camping facilities at the Storm King Dam recreational facility, and camping is not allowed there. There is a caravan park nearby.

For the nearby caravan park and others, see Southern Downs & Granite Belt caravan, camping and holiday parks, or Where can I camp in the region?

items.q: Can I stay overnight in a Council park?
items.a:
Yes, in 3 parks, for limited periods:

  • Dalrymple Creek Park, Allora Drive, Allora: 24 hours
  • Leyburn Sports Grounds, Tummaville Road, Leyburn: 72 hours
  • Jim Mitchell Park, McCosker Drive, Dalveen: 24 hours

Tents and self-contained vehicles are both fine. Each park has a sign saying how long you can stay, and the time on the sign is what applies.

These are rest stops, not campgrounds, and facilities are limited.

For longer stays, use one of the dam campgrounds or a private park. See Where can I camp in the region? or our Caravan & Camping Information page.

items.q: Can I camp anywhere else — a roadside, reserve or car park?
items.a:
No. You cannot camp, sleep, occupy or stay overnight in a local government controlled area. The only exception is a park or reserve where a sign says camping is allowed.

This is set by our Local Law No 4 (Local Government Controlled Areas, Facilities and Roads) 2011 and the matching Subordinate Local Law.

Local government controlled area: land, facilities and other infrastructure that we own, hold in trust or otherwise control — anything other than a road.

To find somewhere you can camp, see Where can I camp in the region?

items.q: Where are the caravan dump points?
items.a:
We look after 5 wastewater dump points across the region:

  • Warwick: Morgan Park
  • Allora: Apex Park
  • Leyburn: Sports Ground
  • Dalveen: Jim Mitchell Park
  • Stanthorpe: Apex Park Reserve

Our 2 campgrounds, Washpool Reserve and Connolly Dam, also have a dump point for campers staying there.

To use one, lift the lid of the dump point and lower your wastewater hose into the opening.

Only the 3 Ps go into a dump point: pee, poo and toilet paper. Wet wipes, rags, rubbish, children's toys, tennis balls, nappies, clothing, sanitary pads and tampons, cooking waste and sand all cause blockages. Do not put them in.

Details are on our Caravan & Camping Information page. To fill your water tanks, see Where can I fill my water tanks?

items.q: Where can I fill my water tanks?
items.a:
We run bulk water fill stations across the region. Locations, access and charges are on the Supply of Bulk Water page.

Washpool Camping Reserve also has clean drinking water on site.

items.q: What events are on?
items.a:
The Southern Downs & Granite Belt events listing has what's on across the region, from food and wine events to markets and festivals.

For the region's agricultural shows and their dates, see our Agricultural Shows page.

items.q: Is Condamine River Road open?
items.a:

Never drive through floodwater, however shallow it looks. If a causeway is under water, turn around.

items.q: How do I arrange a burial or an interment of ashes?
items.a:
If you are using a funeral director, they usually arrange the burial or interment with us for you.

To arrange it yourself, contact our Cemeteries team. Or download the Burial Application or Interment of Ashes Application from the Cemetery/Memorial Forms page and send it to us.

You can also reserve a plot ahead of time with a Reserve Application. Reservation fees are not refunded at the time of interment.

In some Southern Downs cemeteries, a second interment in the same grave may not be possible because the ground is not deep enough. Second interments are not available at Eden Gardens or Wallangarra.

Fees depend on the cemetery and the type of plot. Interments after 3.30pm, on weekends and on public holidays cost more. All the fees are in the Cemeteries section of our Fees & Charges.

To book or ask about a burial, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to be transferred to Cemeteries.

items.q: How do I find a grave, or order a plaque or headstone?
items.a:
To find where someone is buried, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to be transferred to Cemeteries. You can also lodge an online service request asking for a grave location.

For a memorial, use the:

  • Memorial Plaque Application for a plaque
  • Monumental Work Application for a headstone or other monument
  • Park Memorial Application for a memorial in a park

All 3 forms are on the Cemetery/Memorial Forms page. Fees are in the Cemeteries section of our Fees & Charges.

items.q: How do I report a maintenance problem at a cemetery?
items.a:
Lodge an online service request. You can use it for mowing, grave maintenance, plaque maintenance, exhumation enquiries, grave locations and general admin questions.

If you would rather talk it through, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to be transferred to Cemeteries.

items.q: Can someone be buried on private property?
items.a:
Yes, under certain conditions and with our approval. The rules are in Subordinate Local Law No. 1.13 (Undertaking Regulated Activities Regarding Human Remains) 2011.

The application needs, among other things:

  • a certified copy of the approval for the burial under the Coroners Act 2003
  • the written agreement of the landowner, and of anyone else with a registered interest in the land
  • evidence of the wishes of the person who died and their relatives
  • details of the family's long-term connection to the land, the burial site, and how access to the grave will be kept in future

Lodge the form and documents at one of our offices. The application fee is in the Cemeteries section of our Fees & Charges.

See Burials on Private Property for the full list of documents and the application form. For help with an application, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to be transferred to Cemeteries.

items.q: Can I put up a roadside memorial?
items.a:
Yes, with our approval. Fill in the Roadside Memorial Application and send it back to us. We will give you our decision in writing.

Our guidelines are there to keep family, friends and road users safe while a memorial is put up and visited.

The form is on our Roadside Memorials page. For help, call us on 1300 697 372 and ask to be transferred to Cemeteries.
